speechtext: Not yet for a moment. I expected the Prime Minister to intervene here. The divisions of this county, as proposed in the Bill, are so obviously at variance with reason, that it shall not be necessary for me to do more than make a very short statement. It would be a waste of time to bring evidence to prove that two and two make four, and so I shall only submit a few facts. I sent to the right lion, gentleman a map showing the division of the county, as proposed in the Bill, and also the division which I suggest. The county of Kent is divided nearly equally territorially by the river Thames. The city of Chatham is situated on both sides of the river, with the corners of Harwich and Raleigh on the south, and Dover and Chatham townships on the north. Exclusive of the city of Chatham, the population on the south side of the river is 27,338, and the population on the north side, also excluding the city of Chatham, is 20,797. The natural conclusion would be-apart of course from political considerations-that the city of Chatham should be put on that side of the river which has the smaller population. Under the present Bill, in one constituency you will have 25,338 and in the other a population of 32,074, or a difference of 6,500.

I shall not have a very difficult task in convincing those who have listened to the remarks of the hon. gentleman and who will listen to mine, that the case is not such as the hon. gentleman represents it to be. I have looked with some attention at this particular riding in view of the very strong representations that havei been made by the hon. gentleman on more than one occasion. This morning he lias referred to the proposed redistribution of Kent in, I think, unwise terms. He said that it was contrary to reason, that it was unfair, that it was manifestly unjust. I

think he will agree with me, on consideration, that it is not possible to apply any such terms to this redistribution, it cannot be said that it is contrary to reason, that it is unshapely, nor that it is unfair or unjust. I grant that there are two ways of looking at this particular question. I grant that upon one point and one point alone my hon. friend has an advantage on his side. Between the distribution which he wants and the distribution which is proposed by the Bill there is quite a difference in population. If the committee were to adopt the division o.f the county which he wants to have, there would be in one riding in round numbers about 29,000 souls and in the other about 27,000. It must be admitted. that according to the division provided for in the Bill, there is a much larger discrepancy, East Kent having about 25,000 and West Kent about 31,000, a difference of about 6,000. It is fair that we should take that point into consideration. But what are the reasons which in my estimation make the division which lias been suggested by the committee one that is fair and equitable and according to reason ? The considerations are these : That the divisions are just as compact in the one case as in the other. In the one case the county is divided by the river with its sinuosities. In the other case it is divided almost by a straight line ; there is just one angle.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Two : there is the angle from south to north-east, and from northeast to south again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend is rather hypercritical, I must say. Of course, if we had a straight line, there would be no angle at all ; but there is only one departure from the' straight line. If my hon. friend wants to be hypercritical, I must admit that if you depart from the straight line at all, you must have two angles. So far I stand correctedi; but there is only one departure from the straight line, and in that respect it is just as fair a division as the other. But what is the reason, why the members of the committee have adopted this division, and not that suggested by my hon. friend ? It is, I apprehend, because it involves much less disturbance in the actual condition of things than the proposed division of my hon. friend. The west riding of Kent, by the division provided for in the Bill, will remain the same constituency as was created by the redistribution Act of 1882. I will not say the gerrymander, since the word grates on the ears of some of our friends on the other side of the House, there will not be any difference whatever. By the Act the county of Kent was scattered all over the neighbouring counties. One-half of it. what is now West Kent according to this Bill, was made a constituency under the name of Kent. Tiie rest of the county, what is called East Kent in this Bill, was distributed into Bothwell and some other ridings. Now, the Bill places Kent within its natural boundaries as provided for by municipal organization, and divides it into two ridings, because it has the requisite population. The West Riding is to remain just as it has been for twenty-one years. My hon. friend cannot deny that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is not important to deny it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If it is not important to deny it. I think it is very important to assert it, because one of the cardinal principles which have been acknowledged to guide us is that we should make ns little disturbance ns possible.

I have compared carefully tile Act of 1882, which I have under my hands, with the Bill, and I find that the constituency of West Kent, as outlined in the Bill, is the same constituency as that which was created under the name of Kent by the Act of 1882. Under these circumstances, I ask the House, would it lie fair or just or reasonable, not to retain a constituency which has been in existence for twenty-one years ? If there is good reason why this should not be done, well and good ; but those who had the framing of this Bill decided as far as possible to retain tiie existing condition of things and that principle ought at all events to commend itself to the Conservative members of this House. It seems to me under such circumstances that the division which lias been adopted is a perfectly fair one. I do not pretend to say that the division which my hon. friend wants is unfair or unjust or contrary to reason. I would not say that ; lmt I say that there is just as much reason, justice, and fairness in the division which has been adopted in the Bill as in the one proposed by my hon. friend. I will go further : I think I can say also, that since you can have two ridings in this county without breaking the boundaries of one, that is the far better plan to adopt.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I would like to ask the right lion, gentleman a question. He has laid great stress on the fact that the riding now called West Kent has been for twenty-one years constituted as Kent ; and he li;Id that it would be an outrage to disturb

it. Tlint was the burden of his argument. Now, if a rule of that kind were laid down throughout, I would say that the right hon. gentleman might very properly lay stress upon it, even though it might not be a good rule. But what does he think of the propo-sil of his committee to disturb the boundaries of Waterloo, which have been fixed f>r a greater number of years ? I would like to ask the right hon. gentleman how he can apply his argument to Kent when he will have to take the very opposite view vdth regard to another riding which he is coming to soon ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, we have not come to the case of Waterloo yet, and I have an open mind with regard to it. I have not looked at the case of Waterloo, but I have looked very carefully at the case of Kent, and it seems to me that the division adopted by the committee is a fair one, and that the Bill would not be improved by adopting the suggestion of my hon. friend.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Of course, we are overpowered and must yield', whether with good grace or with bad grace, to the majority in this House. The right hon. gentleman has an excuse; you never found a man without an excuse. That is the history of the world. Even Adam had an excuse, and I am bound to say that it was neither laudable nor chivalrous^ but he yielded to temptation, as the right hon. gentleman has done. And the excuse the right hon. gentlemaijL lias is utterly destitute of reason or manliness. I have no right to assume that I can get a nomination in that riding if I wanted to. The Minister of Public Works devised the brilliant excuse, in the first instance, that it would bring the hon. member who represents the county now into what would be called North Kent county. That was the only reason he urged ou the committee. He did not say that to do this would be unfair, but he suggested that such would be the case. This arrangement, Sir, was all cut and( dried more than a year ago. The right hon. gentleman knows very well that there is not one riding, commencing at Windsor and ending at Prescott, in the province of Ontario, which could be divided to the advantage of the Liberals that has not been so divided. I challenge the right hon. gentleman to point to one. I shall not discuss this question any further, but shall await with some degree of curiosity to see how the right hon. gentleman will face when he comes to Waterloo. I would like him to remember the defence he has put up in this case. I shall content myself with simply putting on record a motion which I think is in the right direction, and later on I may have something to say about general principles.' I beg to move :
That section 39 be amended by striking out all the words after the word ' the ' in the first line thereof and substituting the following therefor :-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The counity of Kent into two riding' to be called respectively the north and south ridings of Kent.
(a.) The north riding shall consist of the townships of Chatham, Camden, Zone, Dover East and Dover West, the city of Chatham, the towns of Bothweill, Dresden and Wallaccburg, and the village of Thamesyille.
(b.) The south riding shall consist of the townships of Orford, Howard, Harwich, Raleigh, Tilbury and Romney, the towns of Ridgetown and Blenheim and the village of Tilbury.
I recognize that this motion is mere empty form, as the result was very well settled some time ago. Everybody knew that even members of this committee did not hesitate, to say-I have it from reputable quarters-i that I was endeavouring by some shuffle or other to have a constituency shaped for myself.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend, who now is entrenched in West York, always applauds the wrong-doings of his party. It came to my ears from reputable quarters that endeavours were being made by myself and other members to secure constituencies in which we could run. I- want to say that I have asked for no favours at the hands of any party, either my own or the party opposite. I have no right to assume that I could get the nomination in a single constituency in Canada. I have just this to say to the right lion, gentleman, that from east to west of Ontario, he cannot put his finger on one riding which has not been changed to the advantage of the Liberal party where it could be done. It matters not whether he calls such a proceeding a gerrymander or not, the electors will know what to think of it. We are told that this was a conference. It certainly was not in the ordinary sense of the word. A conference, as it is generally understood, is the meeting of a certain number of gentlemen on common neutral ground, where men are bound to stand by what is right, and where they are supposed to carry out the dictates of honour and honesty, but the conference in this case was not of that description. It was simply a committee called to ratify foregone conclusions and adjust the constituencies iu the interests of the government.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has made these wild charges so often that it is hardly necessary to notice them any more. I intimated to him some days ago 'that if we came to discuss the merits of the Bill, he would have no foundation for the statements he has been making. The hon. gentleman submits his amendment in a timid, fearing way, and announces that he does not expect it to be supported. No wonder, for he has no grounds for asking that it be supported. But, lacking good reason for liis amendment, he makes wild changes and loud sounding statements against the committee and against the majority in this House,

statements that have no foundation, and that have been proven to have absolutely nothing in them. In his endeavour to impress the country with the idea that there is really something in the wild statements he has been making for a month or two past, he harps insistently upon this one idea. He has been declaring that this was a most outrageous and. indefensible gerrymander. But, when we come to consider the details of this Bill, though notice has been gtiven tof certain amendment^ ithe hon. gentleman himself has not nerve enough to propose many of them. He knows that a comparison of the proposals contained in those amendments with the proposals in the Bill would show such extreme attempts on his part to gain the partisan advantage for his friends, that he is unwilling that that comparison should be made. He talks about partisanship;. But he knows, as everybody knows, that, while this committee was expected to do what was right and fair as between the parties, it was not expected that the majority would hand over the constituencies of this country to the manipulation of their opponents. The proposals of that committee are before you, Mr. Chairman ; and it is for those who are dissatisfied to show where those proposals are wrong, if they can. It is well understood that the committee was governed by certain principles, but they had to consider conditions and circumstances in reaching their conclusions. What applied to one constituency might not apply to the other. It is no argument to say that a certain thing was done in one case, and so the same thing should be done in another, regardless of the geographical situation and other conditions and other cases. That is ridiculous -I would not like to use stronger language. The proposal of the committee in this case is fair and in the public interest, while the amendment of the hon. gentleman, like several others of which notice has been given, and which, I suppose, will be submitted, is simply designed to secure to hon. gentlemen opposite an undue and unfair advantage from a party standpoint.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am not surprised at the hon. gentleman (Hon. iMr. Sutherland) making that speech-such a finished artist as he is in carving constituencies, and a gentleman who knew exactly what was to be done before he entered the committee. He had no ears to hear, no eyes to see. How can one appeal to the reason and fairness of one who is deaf to reason and common sense ? I admit that I cannot move him. He says that I have made wild statements. That is exactly such an expression as I should expect from the hon. gentleman. No doubt the hon. gentleman is well pleased with his work. I can tell him. however, that lie,does not cut so good a figure as he thinks iie does. He may challenge the. admiration of his own friends, but he has not
raised himself in public estimation. Let me remind the members of this committee-one of them, it is understood, ambitious for a seat in the cabinet, and another already holding a portfolio-that in assuming the duties of this committee they took upon themselves a great responsibility, that of carrying out the solemn pledge made by the right hon. Prime Minister. The Prime Minister went out of his way to say to the people : I am going to give you a fair Redistribution Bill. He instanced the case of Mr. Gladstone. I do not know whether he aims to play the role of a Gladstone, but I do know that he is able to imitate every weakness, though I fear that he gives us but a poor imitation of any single virtue possessed by that great man. He said : We are making a new departure ; we propose to have an end of gerrymanders and to make a fair redistribution. I do not know whether the members of the committee who undertook to carry out the right hon. gentleman's promise mistook what the right hon. gentleman said, or whether they felt that, notwithstanding what he had said, notwithstanding his solemn pledge, they were at liberty to do as they pleased. And they come back to the Prime Minister with a measure which must he acceptable to politicians of their stripe, but involving acts for which not one of these gentlemen would care to be responsible in private life. But I am told that these are wild statements. I put a simple ease, and would not have repeated it had not the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) sat down without having made the slightest reference to the challenge I offered. I challenged the hon. gentleman : Put your finger upon one constituency in which you could gain a party advantage that you have not taken means to gain. If this is a wild statement, it is easy to point out the single instance which I challenge him to give.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have pointed it out so often.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has often tried to point it out, and he has appeared ridiculous as often as he has made that attempt. I can understand hon. gentlemen opposite saying, whether they had any foundation for it or not : You who are now in opposition perpetrated scandalous gerrymanders in 1882 and 1892 : yon deprived the Liberal party of their rights ; and we propose now to retaliate, because it will be a good lesson to you. If they were to take that course, while I could not say it would be a commendable course, it would at least have the merit of courage, and of such honour as mere courage shows. But when they make a pretense; when they tell us that the struggle between parties in these matters should cease ; when they ask us to sit down in conference with them ; and when we find that there is not a single proposition for their own party benefit on

which they could agree among themselves which has not been carried out-what can we think of their conduct ? They invited us as men of honour to confer with them, declaring that they wished to deal with these matters in the public interest, declaring that though they have the majority they will not take advantage of it, but that we would settle this question as it had been settled in England, and would make a redistribution that would forever reflect honour upon the Prime Minister, who proposed this method of action. What occurred in England ? Was there any murmur of unfairness ? Was there a majority committee in England ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There was.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There was a majority upon the committee, but there was no majority report. There was not a murmur of polities in it. It was not a committee in name only in England, but in fact ; it is one only in name here. It is bad enough to take the course that is taken, but it is infinitely worse to add hypocrisy to it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend is serious in the wild and extravagant language he has just used, let me tell him, and I appeal to lion, gentlemen on both sides of the House, that he has selected as the occasion for such language the weakest point there is in the Bill, because if there is in this Bill a disposition which is fair and is above criticism, it is the very disposition of the county of Kent which he is now criticising. The bon. gentleman said a moment ago that I could not put my finger upon a single constituency which had not been arranged for party advantage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, 1 said there was not one in which it was possible to take a party advantage in which it was not done.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Even with that qualification, the hon. gentleman's statement is wholly incorrect. The hon. gentleman says we have not changed any division in which we did not take a party advantage ; but it happens that the very riding we are discussing at this moment, although there has been a change made in it, is now made just as it was left by his own friends in the last redistribution, and still the hon. gentleman complains of what we are doing. Because in 1882 the Conservative party gerrymandered the county of Both well for party advantage, he is now complaining because we do not leave it as it was before. Let me refer him also to the county of Peterborough which, upon the testimony of the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), gives us a chance of losing one member by the redistribution we have made. In Toronto we have made, a new riding-has that been done for the benefit of the Liberal party ? Is it not well known that it is likely to return a Con-Mr. CLANCY.
servative ? What would he have said if we had treated Toronto as we do Mont real, making no change in it, although Montreal is more strongly Liberal than Toronto? But we will not do for Montreal what we are doing for Toronto. This is all the credit we get for having been fair to hon. gentlemen opopsite. Mr. Chairman, I begin to regret that I did not do ns some of my friends here wanted me to do, and that when we bad it in our power to gerrymander our friends opposite in the same way they gerrymandered us, we did not take advantage < f our opportunity.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 1 assume that the Bill so far as Kent is concerned, needs no defence, as I am sure that this is the only reasonable disposition that could be made of the county of Kent, and I have never heard a single man in the county of Kent even attempt to make such a proposition as to divide it by the river, as suggested; by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). He said' the other day in his speech that the riding of East Kent was sixty-five miles long. I have taken considerable pains to make an inquiry, and I find that the longest straight line through the riding does not exceed forty-three miles. In fact, the riding is twenty-five miles square as near as possible, leaving in West Riding in about the same position, 25 miles square on tire average. The riding divided by the river, as he proposes, would make the south riding fourteen miles wid'e and not less than fifty miles long. So I say the division he proposes would put both ridings in a worse shape than they are now, and would take away from the people the advantages they have been heretofore enjoying. The riding as it is now will have the shape it has had for twenty-one years. The county of Kent has agricultural societies, East Kent has one and West Kent lias one; it has collegiate institutes, East Kent lias one and West Kent has one.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is it the East Kent and the West Kent, as now constituted, that have these agricultural societies, or are they local societies ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Yes, as proposed by the Bill East Kent and West Kent will have these societies. East Kent as proposed by the Bill takes in the townships of Orford and Howard ; they are in East Kent. West Kent holds its agricultural meetings in the city of Chatham, which is in the riding of West Kent; while East Kent holds its meeting in the town of Thamesville, which is in East Kent. The collegiate institute in the town of Ridgetown is in East Kent, and the collegiate institute in West Kent is in the city of Chatham, which is also in West Kent. The hon. gentleman says that this change was cut and dried a year ago. I never heard of a proposal to divide the riding by -the river until I heard it from the

lion, member himself. 1 never heard either man, woman or child in the county of Kent propose such a division as that, and I do not think that one man in fifty in the riding would think of proposing such a thing, or would be willing to adopt it if it were proposed. I think the proposition made in the Bill is the only one that could be adopted by any man of common sense.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Let the hon. gentleman divide it by its proper boundaries and take the responsibility of going home andi fighting it out. The hon. gentleman is sheltering himself behind the committee. I do not blame the hon. gentleman for grabbing tiie plums and putting them in his pocket, he is getting all of them. Now, let the lions gentleman divide Kent fairly. He is in the city of Chatham, let him go into the riding as it is constituted to-day and fight his battle there like a man, instead of standing behind a wall and throwing stones.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I made no proposition whatever to the committee; in fact, I do uot think any proposition needed to be made to a sensible committee. Of course, I am getting used to the hon. member for Botli-weli scoring me. Only a few days ago lie made an attack upon me which was ungentlemanly, uncalled for and untruthful.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Order.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman lias no right to say that I made an ungentlemanly and untruthful attack upon him, and I ask him to withdraw those words.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 1 was not listening and did not hear those words, but if the bon. member for Kent used them lie will please withdraw them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I withdraw the word ' untruthful,' but his statements were not correct.	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I would not have taken part in the discussion with reference to Kent were it not for some observations made by the leader of the government. My hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) a few moments ago challenged the government to point to a 'single riding where it was possible for them to take a party advantage and where they had not taken it. The right -hon. gentleman, in answer to that, said that according to the hon, member for South Lanark they had a chance of taking a party advantage in East Peterborough, and they had not done so. The two idaces that he mentioned were East Peterborough and Toronto. In Toronto he said they had an opportunity of gaining a party advantage by leaving Toronto with the four members it had before. What foundation was there for the right hon. gentleman's remark in reference to East Peterborough ? Was it possible that they could take a party advantage there and that they did not take it ? The question did not arise at all. A statement
was made in reference to East Peterborough when the question of Carleton. and Leeds and Broekville came up. I said, that, in the first place, In order to accomplish a compromise, the minority upon the committee consented- that Carleton should have one member, that on account of Gloucester and Osgoode having formed since 1805 a portion of the county of Russell and in the British North America Act being mentioned as a part of the county of Russell, we consented that Russell should remain as it is although Carleton under the scheme of the limitation would be entitled to two members. We put back the two townships of Fitzroy and Huntley and we were a consenting party to this arrangement upon the understanding that Leeds and Broekville should receive, in compensation for the member we lost in Carleton. three members. In reference to East Peterborough, although perhaps it was not a part of the agreement, the proposition was made, I think, by the hon. Minister of Justice (Hon.. Mr. Fitzpatrick) that the township of Monaghan should be added to East Peterborough for the purpose for bringing up tbe numbers in tbe calculation. It was only informally mentioned and there was no agreement come to about East Peterborough. But, I was a consenting party to thei addition of Monaghan to East Peterborough, notwithstanding the fact tttiat it belonged to another riding. We were a consenting party to that addition and to the proposition that Peterborough should have two representatives, What kind of an answer is it for the right lion, leader of the government to get up and in reply to my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) say that according to the statement of my hon. friend from South Lanark lion, gentlemen opposite could have exercised a political advantage, but that they did not do so ? There is not a scintilla of argument, there is nothing logical to support the right hon. gentleman In making a statement of that kind. The only logical answer lie made to the challenge of my hon. friend from Bothwell was when he "said : We had the right and the power of limiting tiie representation of the city of Toronto before, but we did not exercise it. We allowed Toronto to- have five members. That is the complete answer to the challenge of my hon. friend but where they have the power of gaining a party advantage in making the delimitation of the counties from one end of Ontario to the other, they exercised it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If there was no logic in my answer it should be a. lesson to me not to base any argument upon a statement made by my hon. friend from South Lanark, because, at page 11048 of the ' Hansard', I find that my hon. friend said :

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Perhaps it would be reasonable for me to explain my position in reference to the county of Carleton. Under the proposition or plan laid down by the right

hon. gentleman,' there is not the slightest doubt that the county of Carleton would be entitled to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Two of the townships belonging to the county of Carleton under the arrangement have since 1865 belonged to .the county of Russell, that is the townships of Osgoode and Gloucester. They were placed in the county of Russell under the British North America Act. The argument of the supporters of the government who were on the committee was that they ought not to be interfered with. We insisted on our extreme rights that Carleton should have two represen tatives, and as a compromise the Minister of -Justice waived the opinion he had in reference to the division of united counties, that is his objection to dividing them apart from county boundaries, and he gave us a member for the county of Leeds, to which it is doubtful if we were entitled.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER (reading)-
-land got in return two members for Peterborough. We consented to Peterborough, and in that respect I think the hon. gentleman is mistaken, because the probabilities are that we will carry the two Peterboroughs.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Did the committee think so ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) having made a challenge to the right hon. leader of the House, the right hon. gentleman, has responded to that challenge by referring to the magnanimity of the government in giving an additional member to the city of Toronto. My hon. friend from South Lanark (Hon. Ml-. Haggart) has disposed of the right hon. gentleman's statement respecting the county of Peterborough. Will the right hon. gentle-; man permit me to point out to him that as far as the city of Toronto is concerned the committee appointed to make the redistribution of seats for this House turned a deaf ear to the representations made by myself and -my colleagues, and will he permit me to repeat what I said last night that the papulation of the city of Toronto to be represented in this House is 64.000 more than the population of Toronto under the Redistribution Bill of 1891 ? Does the right hon. gentleman think he has done justice to those
64,000	people by giving them but one reprej sentative, when the unit of representation for the rest of the province is 24,381 ? Does he think the city of Toronto has received, fair play in having its unit of representation; fixed at 41,608, while the unit fixed for the! rest of the province is only 24.381 ? Does my right hon. friend think that one scintilla of justice or fair-play has been given, or that an equal division of the) city of Toronto has been made by the method which has been adopted of sepa-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
rating South Toronto from the rest of the city ? Does the right hon. gentleman think that there is anything chivalrous or manly about a division 200 yards wide' in some places, 100 yards 'wide in other places and which extends for five or six miles along the city front ? Does the right hon. gentleman think for one minute that he holds up the example set by the right hon. W. E. Gladstone or by Lord Salisbury by the delimitation of the boundaries of the city of Toronto ? There is one thing and one thing alone that the city of Toronto may be thankful for, and that is that the right hon. gentleman and liis friends on the committee did not give it the same measure of justice that his political friends in Ontario did some years ago. When they could not subdivide the city in a way to gain a seat for the Liberal party wliat did they do? They resorted to the effete, played out, tried and discarded system of minority representation. That was the only drop to be added to our cup of iniquity.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think we are wandering away from the, subject under discussion. We are discussing the question of Kent now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, as an old parliamentary hand, that when a city is being attacked, those who have the honour of representing that city should have the right to reply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The case of Toronto will come up in a short time and then the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) will have an opportunity of discussing it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right hon. Prime Minister introduced the subject of the city of Toronto.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: He only referred to the city as an illustration.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) is only giving it as an illustration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The question as to the method of dividing the city and cutting off a strip so many yards wide and so many yards long is not now under discussion at all.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not desire to break the rules of the House, but let me tell the right lion, gentleman that to make the constituency of South Toronto the cemmittee took parts of West York, West Toronto, Centre Toronto and East Toronto. The map of the constituency, as it has been subdivided, will show that what I have said is correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word or two upon this subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Upon what ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Upon the subject before the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I hope the hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) 'will confine his remarks to the county of Kent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly. I shall have something to say about the city of Toronto in due course. The hon. gentleman from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has frequently made the statement that Toronto has been scandalously divided, that it is an outrageous division. I shall not refer to that subject further at present, but I shall have . something more to say in regard to it when we come to that division, and I think we will be able to show that the division that has been made by this <.mmittee is fairer than the one made by tire hon. gentleman and his friends in 1892. In reference to the matter under discussion-Kent and Botli-well-I have only to say, as has been stated by the member for Kent (Mr. Stephens), that the division which has been made by the committee is so fair and reasonable that little need be said about it. We are used in this House to hearing lectures from the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). He is an expert in that business. No member in this House can lecture so volubly, and shake his head so systematically, and spread his hands so wisely, as the member for Bothwell. He has long experience in that. He was elected in Kent in 1879 by 400 or 500 majority, but his course was such that his majority dwindled down from 400 or 500 until he was defeated by as many on the [DOT]other side. The people did not take any stock in him. He lectured1 the members of the legislature until the people of Kent got sick and tired of him. This is his second term in this House, and we all can appreciate what his tactics are worth. His division of Kent county is for the sole purpose of making a safe seat for himself, and no one knows it better than he does. The division we now propose leaves Kent the same as it was in 1882. The Tories thought It was a good safe constituency for them then, and they made the division for that purpose, but the people of Kent found that the Tory doctrine was all wrong, and they now support the Liberal party, and are likely to support my friend Mr. Stephens for many years to come. Now that Kent has become a Liberal constituency, the member for Bothwell would like to change it again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What drove the hon. member from Kent to take shelter in York ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The member for York could have been elected in Kent if lie wanted to. We are taking what is the county of Bothwell and making it east Kent, and we are simply restoring the townships which were taken out of Kent and put in West Elgin.

I hope that I shall owe another election to the Liberal party. Item 42-the county of Middlesex.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Inasmuch as many members on both sides have said at various times that the county of Middlesex has been allowed too many members, I would like to be informed by what method it was allotted the representation given it. I ask this in order that I may make good in the country the action of the committee and the House. I had some misgivings as to our having the right to three members and made inquiries. The explanation I got from the chairman was this, that in arriving at the number he added Middlesex to London, thus making the population 92,000. He then divided that by the unit, which gave three members and over one-half. Therefore London and Middlesex were entitled to four members. Of course the county of Middlesex wants as many members as it can get. It would even take more if it could, and the city of London would also like one more member, but the question arises, what right have we to more than three representatives ? What right has London to two members or less than two V In trying to convince myself that the county of Middlesex is entitled to three members, I feel somewhat at a loss. So far as the delimitation of the county is concerned, that has been done exactly as it should, and as it would satisfy the county, out if I were to be asked why Middlesex should have three 3G3
members and some other county, with a greater population, have not so mauy, I would not be able to give an answer. I find that Middlesex has a population of some 54,700, Wellington has 55,646 and La mb ton 56,642, and Wellington and Lambton have each but two members. Kent, with a population of 57,422 has two members. So has Essex, with a population of 58,516, Bruce with a population of 59,020, and Hastings with a p ipulation of 59,291. The chairman of the Redistribution Committee explained the other evening that he arrived at his conclusion by adding the population of London and Middlesex together, which made something over 92,000 and which divided by the unit gave four members. He then took London and gave it one member and gave three to the county. This to my mind was an arbitrary action-separating the city of London from the county after adding it to the county. If the chairman will explain that, I shall be satisfied and will -stand up for the rights of Middlesex; but If ,t cannot be explained, I will say to the county, you are entitled to no more than two members, and you have no right to rob another municipality of the full representation it is entitled to. Take London, with Its population of
38.000	from the county and you have the population of the county 54,700. Dividing that to give the three members, you will find that one constituency has 16,200 the other
18.000	and the other 20,000. That with
16.000	is the third lowest riding in population in Ontario, although there are two constituencies in the province of Quebec with less than 10,000. The question is this : By what rule-do you add the city of London to the county of Middlesex and then arbitrarily take it away and give it one member andi then give the other three members to Middlesex ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Might I ask the how. gentleman by what rule he subtracts London first 7

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is like the Irishman. Instead of answering the question, he asks another. I am asking by what rule you have added Middlesex and London together so as to get four members and then arbitrarily separate Loudon and give it one and the county three. I want to stand for all the representation the county of Middlesex can get, but I do not want to have any man able to cast it up against me that we have more than we are entitled to.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We never took London,away from the county of Middlesex but dealt with Middlesex as we found it. In dealing with the county of Middlesex, the committee took exactly the same course as in dealing with any other county In which there is a city entitled to representation, except the county of York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Except Braut.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, there are two members for Brant.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: How does that apply to Ottawa, Kingston and Hamilton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will give the figures. The unit of representation agreed to in committee was 36,572 for two members; 60,353 for three members; 85,333 for four members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: How did you agree on these figures ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Has the county within its own boundaries four members at the present time ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) entered the Chamber, I explained that there were additions of about 11,000 to the population. Those who heard all I said will understand that I did not mean taking two members away from the territory within the county limits.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Of course, the hon. gentleman must count those added to the Middlesex constituency.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have nothing more to urge witli regard to the county of Middlesex. I am prepared to justify what the committee have done, not only in the county of Middlesex, but in the city of London. I feel quite sure that the people of London, irrespective of politics, if the matter is fairly and justly put before them, will agree that the best thing has been done under the circumstances. Taking into consideration all the circumstances of the case, taking into consideration that there is no way by which you can deprive Middlesex of another member, the whole question resolves itself into the question whether we were right or wrong in the division we have made, and for my part, I am prepared to justify it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It seems to me the hon. gentleman's attitude is ba-sed upon two inconsistent propositions. In the first place he takes the county of Middlesex as a whole, irrespective of the fact that there is a city within its boundary, and he says it shall have four members. Then in the next breath, for the purpose of justifying 363J
himself, he divides it into two distinct parts, the city of London and the rest of the county, and says you must take the rural part of the county and regard that as distinct from the urban part of the county. Now which position does he adhere to ? Where there is a city like London, Hamilton and Ottawa, do you regard the rural constituency as absolutely the same as if there were no city within its boundaries ? You have here a county with a large city within its boundaries. Are you to deal with it in that way, and to have no regard in fixing the representation, to the fact that there is a distinct and important city within its limits ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman knows what my position is. He was not in the House when I made my statement with regard to Middlesex as a whole being treated just the same as all the other counties in which there are large cities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: He is not treating Middlesex the same as all the counties in which there are large cities, because there is the county of York containing the city of Toronto

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I excepted York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend always brings in exceptions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, in speaking to-day I expressly excepted the county of York, for well known reasons.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend can make his position absolutely safe if he introduces a sufficient number of exceptions to make his position sound and logical, a sufficient number of jualifieations, but without that he cannot do it. He talks* about the representation of the cou'utv of Carleton. I never heard about the representation of Carleton including the city of Ottawa, but I have heard about two members for the city of Ottawa, and I have heard about the representation of the balance of the county, while I do not remember to have heard about Carleton as a whole including the city of Ottawa. I have heard about the representation of the city of Hamilton, and of the balance of the county of Wentworth, or what we call the county of Wentworth, because they are two distinct municipalities ; but I do not think that the committee proceeded very much upon the principle that the county of Wentworth should have three members, and then dividing it up as if there was no city within its limits. These are two absolutely distinct municipal units. Yet the whole basis of the argument of my hon. friend is that you should not have regard to these municipal units in the first place, but that you should take the county of Middlesex as including the population of London and deal with it so that it shall have four members. Well, if that is the law, let us understand it.

Let us understand why the county of York should not be dealt with in that way. Has my hon. friend from London suggested any reason why the county of York should not be dealt with in that way? I did not hear him. But I know of no reason why you should deal with a city like Hamilton in one way and with London in another way, and with Toronto in another way. It is true that the population of Toronto is two or three times that of Hamilton, but is that sufficient to suggest a distinction in principle? Toronto contains 290,000 people, the city of Ottawa contains 60,000 or 70,000 ; well, are you to say that there is a principle applicable to the one case by which the city shall be regarded for redistribution purposes as a part of the county, and another principle in the other case by which another city shall n6t be regarded as a part of the county for redistribution purposes ? I would like to know the principle upon which this is based. As I said before, here are two absolutely distinct municipal units-my hon. friend does not deny that, I hope-the county of Middlesex and the city of London. I speak of the county of Middlesex in the broad sense, I do not know into how many municipal units it may be divided.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman to ask me if I deny that they are absolutely separate municipally. I do not deny it, but they are jojned for judicial purposes, having the same court, the same jury, the same judge.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Does that distinguish it from the city of Toronto in that way ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have answered the hon. gentleman's question.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not gather from what he has just said that he does seek to distinguish it in that way.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did seek to distinguish it from the county of York, and when York is under discussion I am prepared to give my reasons for advocating a different treatment of the two places.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I am told by -gentlemen who are more familiar with the facts than I am that York is not distinguishable in that way, because the same practice prevails in the city of Toronto, and even the court-house is kept up as a municipal institution in both Toronto and London. It should be apparent that we cannot distinguish in that way, and that is the only suggestion that I have heard why there should be a distinction. He may say he will reserve his discussion until the city of Toronto comes before us, but I should think that now is the time to discuss this question, because he is taking a very important stand. He says : Here is a county containing a large city, and for the purposes of redistribution we regard that as one unit ; but Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
the principle which has been suggested from this side of the House is that inasmuch as here is a large and important city, municipally distinct in almost every respect, you are not to regard the county as one unit but as composed of two units, and should deal with it accordingly, and you; should apply that principle, not only to thef city of London, but to Ottawa, Hamilton,' Toronto and Kingston. Now, it would seeni to me at first blush that the proposition put; forward on this side of the House has the merit of logic, has the merit of applying the same principle all over, and that itt would be incumbent upon my hon. friend to distinguish between the case of the county1 of Middlesex and the case of the county of York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
There is no better proof than this discussion that the committee were wise, in their manner of dealing with these questions. It is perfectly true that we decided to treat the city of Montreal and the city of Toronto arbitrarily. The reasons have been given for that a.ction. There is no reason why any distinction should be made between the county of Middlesex and any other county. A rule was adopted, and under that rule Middlesex is entitled to four members.
I think there are good reasons for it, and when we come to discuss the city of Toronto it will be more in order to give those reasons. All the other counties in the province having cities of greater or less population than Toronto, have been treated in the same way as we propose to treat Middlesex.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I should like to make my position clearly understood in asking the question which I do. All I want to know is what rule was applied .to the redistribution of London and Middlesex, in order to ascertain the number of members to which that city and county were entitled, because if hon. gentlemen" opposite can make it clear to me that the same rule has been applied t:>
London and Middlesex as that which has been applied all over the province of Ontario, I am imepared to vote against my partv on this question. If hon. gentlemen opposite can show me that any rule laid clown by the right hon. Prime Minister for the guidance of the committee in carrying out the redistribution of the seats of the Dominion has been applied to the case of Middlesex and London, I am prepared to sustain the government against my own party, but if that cannot be shown, and if these hon. gentlemen to my right and to my left claim a member upon the ground that tlie greater population which they have in their constituencies entitles them to it. then I will have to fall into line, I am afraid, in order that I may keep myself right with myself. I am prepared to be right with myself rather than be right with my party. It seems to me that the more that is said about this arrangement the worse it gets.

There has been too much said about the fairness of this redistribution and about the justice that has been given to every one. There has been too much virtue claimed on the other side of the House, because generally the more we hear about this the' less we see of it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend has made a very fair proposition, I think. If it can be shown to him that the county of Middlesex has been treated the same as all the other counties in the province, irrespective of Toronto

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The lion. Minister of Public Works is a fair man, I know, and I do not wish him to misunderstand me. I do not wish him to understand me as saying that the province was dealt with in accordance with a rule or agreement. I know that the committee started out with an agreement. What I would like to know is if that agreement was carried out.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is what I was going to point out to my hon. friend. It was decided to deal arbitrarily with the city of Toronto and the city of Montreal in considering the redistribution. That settles that point. Whether we were right or wrong, I will not say ; but, as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has pointed out, this is a subject which has been discussed and which can be discussed again.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Wliat does my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) mean by saying that it was agreed ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I said it was decided. T remember the hon. gentleman's proposition, which was to deal with Toronto arbitrarily and to give It five seats.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My first proposition was to take the cities of Ontario, combine their population, deduct that from the total population of the province, and fix the unit for the balance of the province on that basis. That was my proposition in the first instance, but it was voted down.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend, I think, must have been pleased that it was voted down. I think a majority of the House and the country would decide that it would not have been as fair a rule as the one we have adopted. But I was going to answer my hon. friend from East Middlesex. We dealt with these two cities arbitrarily, and in doing so I think the majority on both sides of this House would say that we acted properly. It has been the practice in times past, when dealing with these cities, to deal arbitrarily with them.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Surely, now, the hon. gentleman is not going to fail back, after all the statements we have listened to for the
last week about the methods adopted in previous redistributions, upon the argument that something was done ten or twenty years ago ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In this particular case I think it was right. This principle always received my support. I was pointing out to my hon. friend from East Middlesex that I think it is a clear and distinct answer to his question as to whether Middlesex should be allowed the number of members that is proposed in this Bill to say that outside of Montreal and Toronto, Middlesex has been dealt with by applying to it the same rule that was applied to all the other counties in the province. Therefore, I say this proposition is entitled to his support.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If it lias been dealt with as all other counties in the province have been dealt with, was it dealt with in accordance with the rule laid down by the right hon. Prime Minister ? Was the rule of adherence to county boundaries carried out ? The city of London and the county of Middlesex are as distinct as the hon. gentlemen themselves. There are partnerships existing between them of various kinds, but they are quite as distinct municipally as two separate counties are. While I am saying this, Mr. Chairman, [ am not complaining personally at all, and it could not be put in such a way as to make it appear that I am complaining from a personal standpoint. I am merely putting the question for the purpose of ascertaining what excuse these lion, gentlemen had for the proposition they make in regard to the Middlesexes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend says that the city of London is a distinct municipality from the county of Middlesex. The same statement applies to the case of Windsor, Woodstock, Stratford, Belleville, Hamilton and Ottawa, so that there was no exception made in the case of London. I want to point out to my hon. friend that the hon. leader of the opposition, as a member of that committee, in submitting liis memorandum, went a great deal farther, and if his rule had been adopted the committee would have had to join Middlesex with London whether they wished to do so or not. The city of London is so situated geographically as to make it Impracticable to deal with it in any other way than that in which it has been dealt with. My hon. friend made one very good point in his speech in regard to the dividing of the four constituencies within the boundaries of Middlesex, including the city of London. The large population of the city of London seems to be somewhat inconsistent with the smaller population of some of the rural constituencies. I myself rather felt that the portion of the city which has been for years a part of one of the rural constituencies might have been left in it.

That rule was followed in some other counties, but the chairman of the committee felt that the rule that urban population should be kept together ought to be applied in this case, and perhaps, as the representative of the city, he personally felt more delicate about dividing it than he otherwise would. I think that the majority of the committee rather agreed with me that It would have been a proper position to have taken, violating no rule, to have allowed London Bast to remain in Bast Middlesex. I would have been perfectly agreeable, and if it had not been for the request of the chairman of the committee, I have no doubt that the Bill would have (been brought down in that way. Notwithstanding the inequality of population, there is a good deal to be said to sustain the position of the hon. member for London. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Gilmour) made another statement, which was a very manly and proper one, but he misunderstood me if he says that I, or any other member of the majority on the committee, claim any special virtue for ourselves. I never claimed any particular virtue with regard to this matter-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I referred to the government, who, when bringing down their Bill, stated that they were going to be fair and that the redistribution was to be conducted on different lines from that of any other redistribution, when I know in my bones that you have made a capital job of it for yourselves.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am pleased to know that my friend and neighbour (Mr. Gilmour) is satisfied that we have made a capital job of it, and I am glad that I have not lost the good opinion of the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The government and their supporters started out with the principle that the member,s for city constituencies should represent a larger population than; the members for rural constituencies. They) applied that rule to Toronto, and made the unit 41,608 as compared with 21,540 in the county of York. They made the unit in London 37,976, and the unit in the adjoining Middlesexes 18,242. They applied the rule to London and to Toronto. But in the city of Ottawa they have two members, each representing a unit of 28,820 and in tliel county of Carleton they have one member representing 36,976. Their rule was turned upside down there. In the city of Hamilton they have each of the two members representing a unit of 26,317, but they have the member in the county of Wentworth representing 500 people more in that rural constituency than does either of the members for the city of Hamilton. Therefore, the rule applies in Toronto and London, but it does not apply in Ottawa and Hamilton. It is the same way with the city of Kingston as compared with the county of Fron-tenac. The member for Kingston represents a population of 19,788, while the representative for rural Frontenac represents 24,746. Therefore, out of the five cities affected, three of them are outside the rule laid down by the government. When the Minister of Public Works talks about the sacredness of the rule, he knows very well that they have violated it at every turn. If you lay down a rule, carry it out, as far as possible, but the fact is that you are violating it whenever it suits you to do so.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I confess that I am surprised at the attitude of our friends on the opposite side of the House. Back in 1882, they were not so anxious to protect Middlesex from having too many members as they are to-day. The county of Middlesex, including the city of London, then had a population practically the same as at present, and although the average population was very near the unit, these gentlemen were not satisfied that the county of Middlesex should have three representatives and the city of London one, but they added another member. We had in North Middlesex at that time, a population of 21,239 ; in East Middlesex, 30,600 ; in West Middlesex, 21,496, and in the city of London, 19,746, making a total of 93,081, or a unit for the four members of 23,270. Our friends on the opposition, not being satisfied with the representation of the county of Middlesex, as then constituted, they took from the county of Huron the township of Stephen and the town of Exeter, and added them to North Middlesex. They took Eu-phemia from Lambton and added it to West Middlesex, and they took the township of South Dorchester from Elgin and added it to East Middlesex, thus adding a population of 10,000, and making the total a little over 103,000, or an average of 20,400 for the five ridings. They took from four different counties in order to add a population of ten or eleven thousand, and instead of having an average for each member of 23,270, which was about the unit, they reduced it to 20,400. Some of our friends opposite now say that we are reducing the population of Middlesex to too small a figure. I cannot see for the life of me, why the county of Middlesex, including as it does the city of London, should not be treated in the same way as other counties that contain large cities. Wliy is it different from the county of Elgin, with the city of St. Thomas, although the population of St. Thomas is a little less? Wiiy is it different from the county of Hastings, with the city of Belleville in it? Why is it different from the county of Brant, with the city of Brantford in it? Why is it different from the county of Oxford, with the city of Woodstock in it ? I cannot understand what is the difference between the county of Middlesex and the other counties which have cities, although the cities are somewhat smaller. The city of London is the county town of Middlesex; the county council holds its meetings there; the administration of justice is carried on here, and is paid for by the county and the city combined; and the population of each of the four ridings in the county, including the city of London, will be about 23,200, very nearly the unit. Therefore, I cannot see why the opposition object to our having four representatives from the county of Middlesex, including the city of London, in view of the fact that we have had since 1882 five representatives from the same county. The hon. member for East Middlesex stated that the population was small in one of our ridings. I find that, according to the census, North Middlesex at inesent has a population of 17,455, while under the present redistribution it will have a papulation of 16,419 ; West Middlesex has at present a population of 15,843, while under the present redistribution it will have a population of 18,079. Only one of these ridings will have less population under thte, present redistribution than it has to-day. Therefore, I think we are entitled to have three representatives from the county of Middlesex and one from the city of London. Why should we divide the city of London and have two representatives from it, as hon. gentlemen opposite desire

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They only ask for one from London.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I understood that they wanted two from London and two from the county, which I do not think would be fair. I think the present redistribution will satisfy every person in the county of Middlesex, and I hope it will satisfy the House as well.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works said that the committee were dealing not with Ontario alone, but the whole of Canada, aud were acting on principles which I suppose are applicable throughout. I would like to give him an illustration by way of comparing the representation of the county of Middlesex with the representation of the city and county of Halifax. The county of Halifax contains 74,662 people, and it elects two members, that is, one member for 37,331 people. The county of Middlesex, including the city of London, has a population ofi 92,602 and it elects four members, that is) one member for 23,150 people. If the county! of Middlesex, including London, were entitled to only three members, it would have! one member for each 30,867 of population, or an advantage over the county of Halifax,

which I have the honour to represent, of a smaller unit by nearly 7,000 people. Now, I am not saying that by way of complaint,' If my hon. friends had been acting upon a principle in the committee, and if they had fired the representation throughout the whole of Canada on that xtrinciple, my owni county might well have been entitled to another member at their hands. I only rise to! point this out for the purpose of showing that if the county of Middlesex, including the city of London, were entitled to only three members, it would still have an advantage of nearly 7,000 over the representation fixed for my own county, and as to( which I have made no special complaint. I say this because my hon. friend from Lon-; don used to suggest sometimes in the committee-I do not know whether he has done so in the House-that I had some special grudge against the county of Middlesex.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. leader of the opposition, with his legal training and his great experience, has been able to exemplify, much better than I was able to do, the ridiculousness of the position taken by the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram), in endeavouring to prove by comparisons of population, that there was something unfair in this particular case. I quite agree with the hon. leader of the opposition that these inequalities do exist, and exist to a greater extent in regard to other districts than they do in' regard to the oties quoted. For instance, he quoted the case of Kingston. Although the county of Frontenac, in which Kingston is situated, has a larger population than the city, I flunk it would have been a great mistake for us to have added any part of that rural population to Kingston for the purpose of equalizing the constituencies. All the conditions of a county have to be taken into consideration in making the division.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) argued that certain other constituencies in Ontario were dealt with on the same principle. I was pointing out that the committee did not apply the principle to the case of London at all. With regard to the province of Quebec, is it not a fact that there are counties there with a population of 75,000 or 80,000, and others with a population as low as 13,000 and even 11,000. I understand that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries represents to-day a county with a population of something like 90,000, and in ail probability, at the next redistribution, ten years from now, it will have over 100,000; and yet it is not touched in this Bill. The whole thing is on the line of inequality.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The argument just put forward by my bon. friend illustrates the difficulties of this subject, and the unwarranted abuse which the government are getting for distributing the constituencies as fairly as we are doing. It Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
is quite true that the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries represents a constituency which to-day has nearly 70,000 souls, and which, in all probability, ten years hence, will have 100,000; and if we were to do as the hon. member (Mr. Ingram) suggests, we would not displease our friends in Mai-sotineuve if we added its surplus population to Jacques Cartier and Laval. If we did that, the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) would not come back here. Therefore, my hon. friend has a very poor way of illustrating his reasons for opposing this Bill. If we were to take him at his word, he would be the first to be sorry for what he had done, and the hon. member for Jacques Cartier would have reason to pray, ' Save me from my friends.' That would be the worst service to his party the hon. gentleman could suggest. But I have to say something more serious to my hon. friend from East Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour). He is a good Scotchman, and I think he has shown a characteristic of his race in saying that he wants three members for Middlesex, if it is entitled to them. That is not only the sentiment of a Scotchman, but a human sentiment. Our difficulty in dealing with the province of Ontario was largely due to the fact that we had to deduct from its representation. My hon. friend will notice that by this Bill the county of Hastings will lose one member, the county of Bruce one, the county of Victoria one, the county of Durham one, the county of Norfolk one, the county of Ontario one, the county of Wellington one, the county of	Middlesex one,
the county of Durham one, and so will the counties of Norfolk, Ontario, Windsor, and Middlesex. But the suggestion of hon. gentlemen opposite is that Middlesex should lose two members. To-day Middlesex has
92,000,	including London, and is entitled to four members. In 1882, it had a population slightly larger, I think 93,000, but 11,000 were added to it from the adjoining county, which gave it a total of 103,000, and it was given five members, or exactly the same proportion to each as it is given to-day. To-day that surplus population of 10,000 or 11,000 is removed and the county is brought back within its natural divisions and given four members, or the same proportion exactly as in 1882. But if you want to give London another member, you would have to cut off a member somewhere else. Where could that be done ? What county is willing to sacrifice itself ? Not Huron nor Grey, nor even Toronto. I appealed to my hon. friend from West Toronto yesterday to sacrifice himself, to curb his natural greed and be fair, but he would not consent. It seems to me that my hon. friend is generally very fair, and to his good opinion I attach some importance, "and I think he should admit that the encomium I have given this Bill is not misplaced at all.

speechtext: I cannot allow tlie right lion, gentleman's remarks about the province of Quebec to go without saying .a few words. speechtext: You have never had any complaint on the score of redistribution to make. But what is the position in Ontario ? The'Ontario government has the power of creating a county in an unorganized district, and the practice in the past has been to create such counties with the view of gaining political support. If the Conservatives were in power in Ontario and a new county had to be created, and if they were to follow the lines laid down by the Liberals, they would create a couuty which would give Conservatives support. What are we doing here ? We are putting it in the power of the Ontario government, whether Liberal or Conservative, to create a county out of a new district which will send a supporter of its party to Ottawa. It is all very well for lion, gentlemen opposite to charge the late Sir John Macdonald with injustice, but we know that the redistribution of 1882 did not hold a candle to the redistribution made by the late Sir Oliver Mowat.

Let me put this case. Suppose the city of Montreal were largely Conservative and was entitled to three representatives. I ask my right hon. friend would he do in the province of Quebec what was done in the province of Ontario '! Would he give the city of Montreal the right to elect three representatives and at the same time say to the electors, each elector will have the right to vote twice, that is to say, vote for two out of three representatives ? Would he call that a justifiable law ? Would he apply the minority rule to the city of Montreal for the purpose of getting a political supporter ? If he will apply it to the city of Montreal and then go out and apply in the rural districts, I would not find so much fault, but to appiy to a city, in which he knows that he could not get one supporter, a minority rule of that character, would be going entirely too far. Yet that is what Sir Oliver Mowat did to Toronto, He applied the minority rule to that city and gagged the electors in order to get a supporter. He said, although you have three
representatives from the city of Toronto, you have practically only one expressing the wishes of the people, because you nave only one of a majority. I am glad to say that there was such hubjbub raised that he was forced to repeal that iniquitous law. Does the right hon. gentleman uphold conduct of that kind ? Does he think that the Conservatives of Ontario have not reason to complain ? That is the kind of treatment to which the electors of Ontario have been accustomed since 1885, and that is why we watch with greater care this redistribution than do the hon. gentlemen representing other provinces.
