That Bill was brought down in the closing days of the/session. The House was as weary of that session as this House is of the present session; and the fact that the Bill passed with scant discussion was due to the circumstance that members were anxious to get away. The Bill was sprung upon them, and it was of a character that required a good deal of investigation and study in order to understand its iniquitous provisions; and not many members of the House had the time to do that or were disposed to do it. Consequently the

Bill passed with a degree of facility that ought not to have been permitted. Now, what was the character of that Bill '! I will not go into detail with regard to it; but I will point out certain broad facts which are sufficient to convince any unprejudiced mild that the Bill was an outrageous one. We had in the election of 1891 a Liberal majority in Ontario of 7,276. There were cast 171,595 Conservative votes and 178,871 Liberal votes; and the results were secured by the manipulation of that gerrymander Bill of 1882-a Bill more outrageous than the Bill which was introduced in the Massachusetts Legislature in 1812 under Governor Gerry, from which measures of that character take their name, a Bill which gave to political outrages and crimes of that klud the name of gerrymander. While we had a majority of the popular vote of Ontario in
1891,	that Bill so arranged the ridings that the Conservatives secured sixty-three seats and the Liberals secured only twenty-nine, though they had an absolute majority of the popular vote. Now, Sir, it would be impossible to introduce a Bill to correct even to a limited degree the iniquities cf the gerrymander of 1882 that did not largely change the representation in this province. The removal of those iniquities would make our Conservative friends feel that they were suffering a wrong, because we would be taking from the robber the prey which he had wrested from us. And they talk about this gerrymander. Why, Sir, the Premier of this Dominion, when this Bill was arranged, insisted on standing by the professions and the principles that were enunciated by the Liberal party with regard to this matter when they were in opposition. He insisted upon respecting county lines, upon respecting provisions which necessarily debarred this party from securing advantages such as had been taken by the government in 1882, and subsequently in
1892.	Take, for instance, my own riding. In 1882. North Norf Ik had added to it Dereham and Tilsonburg, taken out of the heart of South Oxford, lapping upon North Norfolk for about two miles. The only Conservative municipalities in South Oxford were added to North Norfolk, with the expectation of making it a Conservative riding, an expectation which was not realized. If we had acted upon the lines adopted in 1882 by our opponents, and again in 1892. do you suppose that our respect for county boundaries would have been allowed to stand in the way of a judicious arrangement of those two ridings of North Norfolk and South Norfolk, with an aggregation of population higher than when there were added to North Norfolk the two Tory municipalities from South Oxford. Here you have the county of Norfolk with 29.147 inhabitants, and putting these two ridings of South and North together, if we had adopted the policy, even in a limited

posed to give time to the consideration of any measure. Every provision in it we were totally unprepared for. I belong to the old Covenanter stock, and I think I may claim to be as good a British subject as the hon. member from East Simcoe.

At the present time we are discussing the riding of Middlesex, and the hon. member for Simcoe interjects with an argument to the effect that the Redistribution Act of 1882 cannot have been very unfair because the debate was concluded in a very short time. That was the. substance of his argument, sweeping aside the little episodes that occurred. Now, I appeal to the leader of the opposition if he thinks that such an argument as that is relevant to the item we have before us.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will take issue with my right hon. friend on this occasion. Neither the chairman, nor my right 364 J
hon. friend, nor any one else can stop a debate on the ground that an argument presented iis not a good one. The chairman has laid down a rule which I think will lead him Into difficulty. I am most anxious to support the chairman, and I recognize the difficulties of his task. But I am pointing out that he imposes upon himself a very onerous duty in dealing with this matter in the way hte does. He says that a few sentences with regard to a matter may be permitted, and a complete speech on either side ; but that is not to be followed by any further remarks. Now, I do not think a rule of that kind can be made to work in this House. As to what took place yesterday, I do not think I am at fault, because the chairman from first to last regarded that amendment of my hon. friend from South Norfolk as absolutely out of order, and he did not think, so far as I understood, that it was one upon which a vote could be taken. For that reason I said that the only way we could vote upon it under the ruling of the chairman was as arbiters and not as members of the House. Therefore it leaves us in the position I suggested, namely, that w(e were discussing yesterday this very matter, and that discussion, it seems to me, cannot be cut off at the present stage. But what was done this afternoon ? The Minister of Public Works instituted a comparison-that was where the mistake was made-between the alleged gerrymander of 1892 and the present alleged gerrymander. That having been done we have got into this discussion, and having got into it, it will be difficult to shut us off.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As a member of this House I am most anxious to support your ruling, Mr. Chairman. I recognize, as the leader of the opposition has done, the difficult position you occupy on this occasion. I say this as the chief sinner, because I am probably the only member who has been called to order twice in this debate by yourself. I was not conscious of being out of order. So I think I was only following the member for South Norfolk himself who had spoken on his amendment, as well as others on the other side, although I was the only one who was called to order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not call the hon. gentleman to order to-day.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I merely wish to say to the chairman that we are all desirous of submitting to his rulings, and we all sympathize with him in his difficult duties. But I want to submit for his consideration whether a good deal of latitude should not be allowed even in

discussing one of these items. I would submit to you, Mr. Chairman, that as long as the members on either side are referring to other matters by way of illustration or comparison, you might allow them to do so to a certain extent.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am very thankful indeed for the kind advice which is given me by hon. members on both sides of the House, but when I consider it I do not find any definite rule by which I am to be guided. I must either adhere to the rules, which it is my duty to maintain in debate, or I must take the advice of hon. members and allow the debate to go at random. I am supposed to exercise my judgment as to whether the debate is within proper rules or not. I think that every hon. member on both sides of the House will recognize the fact that I have given a great deal of latitude in the discussion of the question ; but when resolutions are placed before the House that are absolutely out of order, I am in duty -bound, in justice to myself and in justice to the House, to rule that such proceedings are out of order, because if I permitted hon. members to place such propositions before the House, I would get myself in such an awkward position that I could never defend myself either at present or in the future. It is much easier for those hon. members on whose shoulders rests no responsibility in regard to the rules of order to give advice than to carry it out. While I am willing to allow a reasonable latitude, I a-m not willing to allow hon. gentlemen to get up and fight over things that took place twenty-three years ago, while we are -making no progress at all. I hope hon. gentlemen will realize the responsibility of the position X occupy, and will stand by the chairman when he is endeavouring to discharge his duty.

speechtext:
What is the population of these two ridings now ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS, The population of East Peterborough is 16,291 and of West Peterborough 20,704.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: South Monaghan lias voted in Peterborough since 1867, and the population ought to be included in ascertaining the representation. As far as the Liberal party is concerned, we would be glad to get rid of South Monaghan, because it has always given a Conservative majority. The reason the committee left it in West Peterborough was to give the Conservatives in West Peterborough a fighting chance for their lives. There has been a great change of opinion in East Peterborough. We have the people so educated there' that a Liberal can easily carry it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It also gives the Liberals of West Northumberland a fighting chance.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Peterborough, without South Monaghan, has a population of 36,066, and with South Monaghan of 36,995. What is the reason for giving that constituency two members, when you give Victoria -and Haliburton, with a population of 38,515, only one member ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend can perhaps give me the reason more easily than I can give him the reason, because lie was a member of the committee and I was not. But the only reason I know of is the reason given by the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart), that it was a compromise.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax!. What was a compromise ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will have to quote again to my hon. friend the language of the hon. member for South Lanark.
of depriving Victoria and Haliburton of two members, because my right hon. friend will bear iii mind that Lanark, with a population of 37,242, has two members ; that Leeds, with a population of 37,976, has two members ; that Brant, with a population of 38,140, has two members, while Victoria and Haliburton, which is larger than every one of these counties and has a population of 38,515, is only given one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I inust point out that that is not what was meant by the hon. member for Lanark. Under the rule adopted. Peterborough was entitled to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: As far as Victoria and Haliburton are concerned. I do not think any one ever pretended that there was a compromise, and even if two members were given to Peterborough as the result of a compromise, it is not within my recollection that that would be any reason

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It is easy for the hon. gentleman to say ' No,'
but the fact is that it was. Let me make this statement in answer to the leader of the opposition. The county of Peterborough

was entitled to two members before the county of Victoria. The population of Peterborough, without the township of South Monaghan, is 36,066, and the county of Victoria had only 31,952.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And Haliburton ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Under the rule, Peterborough was entitled to two members before Victoria, and what we unanimously agreed to as a compromise on that committee, was that if Peterborough were to have turn members the township of South Monaghan would be added.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman state that again ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: After it was decided that the county of Peterborough was entitled to two members, then there was a question as to the disposal of South Monaghan, which is situated in the municipal county of Northumberland, and it was decided that it would be a great mistake to put South Monaghan back into Northumberland, because in community of interest Monaghan was allied with the town of Peterborough. There was no division of opinion as to that. After it was decided that Peterborough should have two members, what the member for Lanark agreed to was that South Monaghan should be left in East Peterborough. Peterborough was entitled to two members before that was done, and it was not because it gave a larger population to Peterborough that Monaghan was added to it. The leader of the opposition is correct in -saying that the county of Victoria with Haliburton, has a larger population than Peterborough, but under the rule, Peterborough was better entitled to two members than Victoria, before Haliburton was added.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I absolutely disclaim that I made any agreement or compromise with regard to giving two members to Peterborough.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There was no necessity for it ; you did not have to make a compromise.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not have to make it, because under the rule' which I proposed, Peterborough, and Victoria and Haliburton as well, were each entitled to two members. Victoria and Haliburton being joined together they were more entitled to two members than Peterborough, because they had 2,000 more population. There is no reason for my hon. friend refusing two members to Victoria and Haliburton except one reason which he knows perfectly well, and which the chairman of the committee knows perfectly well, and there is no need of my referring to it. Peterborough was absolutely entitled to two members under my rule, because the next highest county was Russell, which including the townships of Osgoode and Gloucester, had only 35,166,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
whereas Peterborough had 36,066. There was no dispute as to Peterborough being entitled to two members, but if Peterborough was entitled to two members, then Victoria and Haliburton, having a larger population than four of the other counties which have been given two members, should have received two members also. I have never yet been able to find out from the Prime Minister, why it is, that Victoria and Haliburton, being constituted one electoral district, is awarded only one member, while four counties with a smaller population are awarded two members each. We have, therefore, this glaring inconsistency in the Bill upon which my right hon. friend congratulates himself most heartily ; of four counties with a less population than Victoria and Haliburton, receiving two members each, while the county of Victoria, which had two members in the past, is now cut down to one member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If I understood the Minister of Public Works correctly, the principle adopted with reference to counties was applied to all counties alike, irrespective of whether they were enlarged afterwards or not. It occurred to me that that principle was entirely destroyed in the case of a county which was first given its representation according to the population within its municipal lines, if you afterwards added outside territory to that county. So that the principle was destroyed in the case of Peterborough as well as of Victoria, because the unit of representation was struck before the additions were made to those counties. Now, there were two defects in the proposal, in my judgment. One was that it violated the rule of county boundaries, which was laid down as a sacred principle of this Bill by the right hon. the Premier. The second was that if the principle upon which you ascertained the unit of representation was sound, it could only be applied properly when the full population within the limits of a county was known. Now. we have a township added to the county of Peterborough which ought to have been in that county when the unit of representation was struck; otherwise the principle could not be fairly applied

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to explain this matter as clearly as possible. The general principle which the hon. member for East Grey lays down would apply if there were no-, exceptions. But my hon. friend must remember that the rule was adopted before it was known how it would work out. Under that rule the county of Peterborough was

entitled to two members, unless, as be bas suggested, something else intervened. When the rule was adopted, it was fouud that the county of Peterborough would be entitled to two members, though it was the lowest on the list of counties entitled to that number. My hon. friend will remember that I, as a member of the committee, with a view to equalizing the population, proposed to add the provisional county of Haliburton to the district of Muslkoka. If that had been done, there would have bean no justification for any argument, in favour of Victoria having two ridings as against Peterborough. Subsequently representations were made to the committee, especially by the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) and by the people living in the provisional county of Haliburton, that even if the county of Victoria was not to have two members, they preferred to be added to that county; so that my suggestion to add Haliburton to Muskoka was not adopted. But I submitted, and I agreed with the balance of the committee that probably on the whole it was better to add Haliburton to Victoria. But it was perfectly understood that that would not entitle Victoria and Haliburton to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: With whom was that understood ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In the first place, the strongest representation was made by the member for the riding. When he advocated adding Haliburton to Victoria, I pointed out that they would not be entitled to two members under the rule, as against Peterborough.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Why ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Because, as I have already explained, the rule was adopted before its application was made to the various counties in the province, and Peterborough was one of those counties entitled to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What was the population of Peterborough without the addition of South Monaghan ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Speaking from memory, I think it was 36,066, as against 31,000 for Victoria. When my hon. friend looks at the figures calmly, he will see the position of affairs. If he were living in the county of Peterborough, he would take the same view as the representatives of Peterborough and the people living in that county took, so far as thej could influence the action of the committee. He would stand up for what he considered the rights of the county under the rule that had been adopted. There was no objection taken by any member of the committee to the proposition made by the hon. member
for North Victoria. At any rate, the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart) who represented the province of Ontario for hon. gentlemen opposite on the committee, after discussion, agreed to that as he has stated in his place in the House. Subsequently, the question as to where the township of South Monaghan should be placed was discussed, and it was agreed, as he stated, to depart from the rule of adherence to county boundaries, so far as to allpw that township, which belonged municipally to the county of Northumberland, to be joined to West Peterborough.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In striking the representation of Northumberland, did not the committee take South Monaghan into account'!

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Originally, yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And afterwards they took it off and added it to Peterborough.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I will show that we considered all these matters. For instance, I suggested putting the town of Trenton into Northumberland, and only gave way on the representation of the minority of the committee. Territorially it is a part of the county of Hastings, though it is a separate municipality; but I am informed that in every other respect it belongs more to the county of Northumberland than to the county of Hastings. Notwithstanding the inequality in population, it was urged on the committee that it should be left in the county of Hastings and I submitted to the views of others and granted the request. This inequality of population would not have existed to the same extent in either county if my suggestion had been carried out. But to come back to the point, I think I have made perfectly clear the reasons why Victoria and Haliburton are considered one county and the rule applied why my hon. friend thinks should have been.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned, there was no understanding or agreement that Victoria and Haliburton should be combined and have only one member, and I should be surprised to learn that there was any such agreement on the part of my hon. friend from Lanark. I do not think he would say there was if he were in the House to-night. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works says that this is the application of some rule. It cannot be of any rule I know of, unless we have a rule that where a county and a provisional county are joined together, the population of the combined counties is not to be considered in fixing the representation. But I am not aware that the committee at any time adopted any such rules. The argument which the hon. gentleman has pre-

sented, namely, that you are in the first place to take the county of Victoria, consider its population and assign a member to it, and then join to that a provisional county with 6,000 or 7,000 people, and absolutely ignore the population of that provisional county in fixing the representation, is an argument which has never had any countenance from me. No such rule was ever adopted.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Certainly not.	,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, it is only on such a rule there could be any justification for what has been done. As far as Peterborough is concerned, the rule I suggested to the committee would give Peterborough two members and it would also give Victoria and Haliburton two members. There was no rule adopted which would give Peterborough two members and Victoria and Haliburton one member. There never was such a rule.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman and I agree exactly. The hon. member for Bothwell challenged me very squarely this afternoon for having said that Victoria was entitled to two members under the rule adopted. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition and I agree. He states that under the rule which he himself submitted, and which was agreed to, Peterborough was entitled to two members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes. and Victoria and Haliburton as well.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. member for Bothwell denies that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No; neither Peterborough nor Victoria, standing alone, without any complement being added, were entitled to two members, because they were both under the unit; but under the rule stated by the leader of the opposition, Peterborough would come in as standing closer to the unit, and would be entitled to two members under the second part of the rule. What happened ? The township of Monaghan was added to Peterborough and Haliburton to Victoria, so that both came within the rule. Then the larger one was left out and the smaller one given the representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is no difference at all between us. That is exactly what I have been explaining to the hon. gentleman for a week, and I am glad he has come to see what is right at last. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition and myself agree exactly as to how the rule worked. But the hon. gentleman has been taking the opposite contention.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
No, I repeat that Peterborough was under the unit, and if there was a single county that had one more of population than Peterborough, which was Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
somewhere about 550 below the unit, Peterborough would not be entitled to the two members, but under the second part of the rule, it did come in, if no other stood in the way.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The only question then is why Peterborough should be allowed two members and not Victoria and Haliburton. My hon. friend was wrong in asserting that Monaghan was added for a purpose. It was not added until after it was settled that Peterborough should have two members. I have explained to the hon. member for Grey that if it was not for the arrangement entered into, Victoria and Haliburton would have been given two members in preference to Peterborough, and the leader of the opposition said h'e would reserve the right to move that two members should be allowed Victoria and Haliburton. He has given notice of that as an amendment to the general proposition, but he does not propose to take away a member from Peterborough for that purpose. He would have to take a member from Middlesex and give it to Victoria and Haliburton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not want my hon. friend to use the word ' arrangement ' in any ambiguous sense. So far as I am concerned, there was no arrangement to cive the county of Victoria one member and place it by itself. The resolution which I submitted to the committee would result in Victoria and Haliburton being joined and being given two members. I suppose my hon. friend uses the word arrangement in the sense of some arrangement among the ran. ority on the committee. As far as I was concerned, there was no arrangement.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have always understood my hon. friend to take that position, but I did not understand the hon. member for Lanark to take it, nor do I think he offered any particular objection to the suggestion made by the majority of the committee at the time. There is nothing on record, but I agree with my hon. friend that he never consented that there should not be two members allowed Victoria and Haliburton.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In the proposition submitted by the reform representatives on the committee, I see that Haliburton and Muskolca were united together and were to have one member. I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works who was responsible for the change ? How is it that Haliburton was taken from Muskoka and put on to Victoria ?'

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have just explained as plainly as I could, but will do it again. The hon. gentleman will admit that the proposition submitted by myself was different from what is now contained in this Bill.

The hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. 1 Hughes) was one of the most influential representatives who appeared before the committee and argued whether they were to have two members or not, it would be in the interest of the people of that district that the district should be in Victoria.
I cannot recall all the representations that were made to the committee. But the hon. gentleman's arguments seemed to weigh with the committee, and that is what brought about the result.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If he had not been, I would have referred him to ' Hansard.' The hon. gentleman would-find there that the hon. member for North Victoria informed this committee that he had made these representations to the committee on the Bill as ably and as eloquently as possible, and he expressed the pleasure that those representations had found favour with the majority and that he had succeeded in his efforts to have this change made.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not understand the hon. member to say that either the hon. member for North Victoria (Mr. Hughes) or the member for South Victoria (Mr. Vroo-man) is responsible for this change. If I understand it, these two gentlemen, discussing this matter before this committee yesterday, both expressed themselves in favour of Haliburton beiug joined to Victoria. But in no case did they agree to having only one member-in fact both of them voted last night in favour of giving the county of Victoria with Haliburton two members. So, I do not think the hon. minister can put the responsibility upon either of the representatives of Victoria. The leader of the opposition says there was no arrangement whatever, no proposition coming from this side of the House. Then I think it was fair to assume that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) and his friends on the committee are responsible for this change. What this committee do not understand is how itj comes that Haliburton has been joined to Victoria, making a district with a larger population, and giving to that larger population only one member, while for similar population in the county of Peterborough adjoining it, two members are given. The responsibility not resting with the hon. gentlemen who represent the county of Victoria, and the hon. leader of the opposition stating that the proposal was not made from this side of the House, would it not be fair to assume that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) and his friends on the committee are responsible for it, though it is not in accord with the principles the hon. gentleman laid down ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) is acquainted with the facts and has the record before him. I do not know why he should ' assume ' anything. While he is correct in saying that both hon. members for Victoria favoured giving two members to that county, if they could be had, he is not correct in saying that both opposed the addition of Haliburton to Victoria. On the contrary, the hon. member for North Vic, toria (Mr. Hughes) made the fight yesterday in favour of the addition of Haliburton to Victoria. Was the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blain) present ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
From what ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORIyS. To have Haliburton added to Victoria. Is that not correct ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is correct as far as it goes. But what then ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Well, 929 of a population belonging to Northumberland was taken into account in deciding the question whether Northumberland should have two members or one member, and afterwards put into Peterborough. If the hon. gentleman desired to be fair, it seems to me that the only plan which could have been followed was this :	Take
your county, whatever kind of a county it may be, whether a single county, unit' d counties or a county with some other municipality added, then take the aggregate population, and upon the basis of that decide whether it shall have one, two, or three members. If there was any virtue in the principle at all it should have been sedulously applied. This destroys it. There can be no virtue in the principle if you destroy it by the very act which certainly destroys the calculation upon which the result is based. Had you taken the population of Northumberland at 32,451 after the 929 had been taken away, it could not have had, by the rule laid down, two members, and had you not violated the principle by giving it two members first before taking away a part of the population it would not have been entitled to that representation. Mr. Chairman, when this debate was opened last week, the discussion hinged to a great extent on the county of Waterloo. Unfortunately, I was not present and could not enter into the debate. I was detained by illness. When the right hon. Prime Minister brought down the redistribution Bill he stated that he wished to act fairly between the two parties in this country. I do not wish to doubt that statement. I would prefer to believe he desired to do that. In the debate last week in which the case of the county of Waterloo was discussed he made the statement that if any injustice was done to that county the injustice would have to be righted. This afternoon another statement was made by the right hon. gentleman to the effect that in the county of Kent one of the ridings had been in existence for twenty-five years without any change, and he gave that as a reason why there should be no change. I wish to say, as far as Waterloo is concerned, that in 1851 there was one representative from the united counties of Grey, Wellington and Waterloo. In 1853 the county of Waterloo was first divided into two ridings, and sent two members to this House. From that day to this, these two ridings have been maintained, although we have had many redistributions in the interim, and until a few years ago they sent two members to support the Reform party in this parliament. We have an agricultural society in the south riding, and the south riding is entirely contributory to it. It is the same in the case of the north riding. We have in the south riding of Waterloo, in the town of Galt, an hospital which is supported by the people of Galt, Dumfries, Preston, Hespeler, all in the south riding; and' in the north riding we have an hospital in Berlin, which is supported by the people of North Waterloo. All this community of interest, which have existed for long years, will be changed if this Bill should become law. I now present to the House a map showing the county of Waterloo as it has existed for the last 50 years, and in that division the rural population and the urban population are very evenly divided, there being not more than a difference of 1.200 or 1,500 between the two. In the south riding we have the towTn of Galt, the town of Preston,
the town of Hespeler and the village of Hamburg ; the townships of Wilmot, Dumfries and South Waterloo. In the north riding we have the towns of Wa terloo and Berlin, village of Glenora and the townships of Wellesley, Woolwich and North Waterloo. Last week the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) stated in this House that the population of the county would be more unequally divided under the new arrangement than under the old. The Minister of Justice, who was on the redistribution committee, contradicted that statement, but if bis knowledge of other things connected with the county is no better than that, then we are entirely justified in asking the House to reconsider the proposed division of this county. At present tthe population of North Waterloo is 27,124, and the population of South Waterloo is 25,470, leaving a difference of 1,654. Under the new arrangement the population of North Waterloo will be as follows: Hespeler, 2,457; Preston. 2,308; Waterloo township, 3,606; Berlin, 9.747; Waterloo township, 3,411; Waterloo town, 3,537; total, 25,156. South Waterloo, under the new arrangement, will be constituted as follows ; Ayr, 827; Dumfries, 2,104; Galt. 7,866 ; New Harburg, 1,708 ; Wilmot, 4,944 ; Elmira, 1,060 ; Wellesley, 5,051 ; Woolwich, 4,318, or a total of 27,438, leaving a difference in the population of the two ridings of 2,282, or a difference of 628 more than under the old arrangement. This Bill states that the north riding shall consist, among other places, of the ' village ' of Preston. This statement shows that the committee did not understand the matter, because I can tell gentlemen opposite that there is no such place as the 'village' of Preston: it is a town. I am almost ashamed to show you a map of the new riding, because I believe that the committee has not investigated the matter thoroughly, and I hope the Minister of Public Works will persuade the Premier to reconsider this division of Waterloo county. Here is a map of Waterloo county under the new arrangement. When children go to school in the future, if they are asked to point out South Waterloo, they will have to look- at the top of the map, and if they are asked to point out North Waterloo, they will have to look at the bottom. The member for London (Mr. Hyman) stated in the House that it would be a good thing to have the large towns all in the one riding, but I believe it is better that in a county such as this, the division should be made so that the urban and the rural population should be as nearly equal as possible. I ask the House with every confidence to reconsider the proposed division of the county of Waterloo.

In answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clare). I wish to give to the House the reasons which led the majority of the committee to divide the county of

Waterloo as reported in the Bill. The hon. gentleman is perfectly correct in saying that under the proposed redistribution, North Waterloo would have a population of 25,126 and South Waterloo a population of 27,438, the difference being 2,282. Under the proposition made by the opposition, North Waterloo would have a population of 27,124, and South Waterloo a population of 25,470, the difference in the population being 1,654. It was thought that this difference in the population was not sufficient to weigh against the representations that were laid before the committee in favour of the proposed division. Let me say, that the township of Waterloo, for the first time in its history, has had a population sufficient to entitle it to a member. I have before me the population of the ridings as proposed in the Bill for the years 1881, 1891 and 1901; and I wish to point out the difference in the condition of the divisions when the redistribution was made in 1881, and at the present time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There was no division in 1881: there has been no division since 1853.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Under the British North America Act it becomes the duty of parliament to make a redistribution every ten years, and if any constituency is left as it is, it is fair to assume that good reasons were sufficient to allow it remain unaltered, so that it is a -redistribution to all intents and purposes. I will first give the populations of the so-called present South Waterloo. In 1881 North Dumfries had a population of 3,848; Wilmot, 5,358; Woolwich, 5,524; Hespeler, 5,752; Galt, 5,187. At that time the towns of Ayr, Elmira, and New Hamburg were not incorporated, and were not taken into consideration in the division of the county in which they are situated. The population of South Waterloo in 1881 was 26,909 ; in 1891 it had grown to 29,429; in 1901 it was reduced to 27,438. North Waterloo in 1881 had the following population :	Waterloo township,
7.594; the town of Hespeler, 698; the town of Preston, 1,419; the town of Waterloo, 2,066; and the city of Berlin, 4,054; or a total population of 15,831. So that in 1881, when it became the duty of this House to redistribute, the division of the county of Waterloo was : the towuship of Waterloo, had a population of 15,831 ; the balance of the county, a population of 26,909. I quite conceive that the House at that time could not very well have accepted this discrepancy in population, and could not have made the redistribution which is proposed in the present Bill. Now, let us see what the conditions are in 1901. The population of South Waterloo has been reduced to 27,438; but the population of North Waterloo has grown to 25.156; so that a division making Mr. HYMAN.
the township of Waterloo one constituency, and the balance of the county of Waterloo another constituency, can be perfectly well defended on the ground of population, be: cause there is a difference of only 2,282. Now, let us deal with the growth of the towns. Hespeler has grown from 698 in 1881 to 2,457 in 1901; Preston, from 1,419 to 2,308; Waterloo, from 2,066 to 3,537; and the city of Berlin, from 4.054 to 9,747. So that at the present -time th-e township of Waterloo has an urban population of 18,049, which is quite sufficient to entitle it to a member, even without taking into consideration the rural population of the township. In addition to this, I have only to point out that the committee took into consideration the fact that the towns of Hespeler, Preston, Waterloo and Berlin are all in the same township; their community of interest is very great; they are large manufacturing towns; and it was felt that the conditions having so changed since 1881, it was only right and proper that the township of Waterloo should have the representation to which it is entitled.

Yet, that was departing from county boundaries, and, I suppose, having regard to the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, that departing from county boundaries is quite as serious a matter as departing from the principle of not dividing townships. Under these circumstances, he has made no defence at all of the extraordinary division of Waterloo. What could be more impressive than this picture of the gerrymander that has been presented to us by the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) tonight ? Does my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) congratulate himself on that result ? Will he point to this as one of the instances in which he has been simply undoing a wrong that was done in 1892 or 1882 ? That was the theory he propounded when he introduced this Bill-that the sole object the Liberal party had in view, according to his solemn statement, was to undo a wrong that had been done by the Tory party in 1882? What wrong' was done in 1882 with regard to this county that has been righted by this arrangement ? Will my right hon. friend stand up in his place and say that this is as fair a division of the county of Waterloo as the one that has prevailed for the last fifty years ? And does he attach no significance to the fact that by this arrangement, this extraordinary, this unheard-of arrangement, he is hiving a Tory majority of nearly 1,100 in one riding? And my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman) tells this committee that if it were not a shock to his nervous system to divide the township of Waterloo, he would he prepared to do perfect justice to the people of that county. We will accept the hon. gentleman's statement in the parliamentary sense: but we have some idea of the motive that suggested to the majority of the committee this hiving of the 1,083 of a Tory majority by making such a riding as was shown in the pictures presented to us this evening, the notice that suggested the hiving of a Tory majority of 1,650 in the riding of West Hastings-and I say, in passirtg, that my recollections of the shape of West Hastings is that it is almost as peculiar as that of the riding presented to us by my hon. friend from South Waterloo. Let us be at least as sincere as we can with each other in this matter. For the sake of honesty, do not let us contend that any honest principle has been involved in making such a division as was shown to-night. Let us admit on both sides that this was done for partisan purposes. But do not let us go to the people of this country and pretend that any motive of fairness, of justice, of equity, ever actuated any party in making such a division of any county as that. If we are to have a partisan redistribution of the province of Ontario, let us understand it, let us admit it; let us not, in the face of such pictures as that presented to the House to-night, tell the people that our

only object in dealing with tins matter was to undo the wrongs the Tories did twenty years ago. Surely my right hon. friend, after hearing the statements that have been made with regard to this township to-night, after seeing the picture of this county as redistributed by the gentlemen whom we put upon this committee, will not persevere in. the assertion he made when he introduced the Bill to this House, that the only object was to undo certain wrongs done in 1882. This wrong in Waterloo, if it was a wrong, had been going on for fifty years, and no abjection whatever was made to it, so far as I am aware. It involves the division of the county of Waterloo along lines which are perfectly plain and distinct. The division which has existed and which it is now proposed to change, is, for the most part, a natural division. It has been made along the same lines and for the same reason that has taken the township of South Monaghan into a county to which it does not belong, the same principle which has led to the division of a township in the county of Brant. But it was thought a desirable thing to hive 1,188 of a Conservative majority in one of the ridings established in this county

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am surprised-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
