maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: You left that to the' chairman.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I may have left it to anybody. But what I say is true. I do not think the hon. gentleman's figures are correct.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I must say that the statement that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) has just made gives me almost as much of a shock as that experienced, by the hon. member for London at the idea of dividing this township. Under the circumstances, I think I shall be obliged to-take a sip of water.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Hard to swallow.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I must say that up to the present time, I have been under the impression that the Minister of Public Works paid some slight, some trifling, attention to matters of that kind in connection with this redistribution. It is, of course, quite possible that his researches into that question did not lead him so far as the county of Waterloo. I confess I should not have supposed it to be the case, if he had not given me his solemn assurance across the floor of this House, that he had not the slightest idea of the political complexion. Under the circumstances, I think that this is a county, at least, to which my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) should give some slight consideration. I do not think there could be any possible reason for changing the state of affairs that has existed in that county since 1850 or 1853. And I am informed-what I did not know before-that the division of this county was suggested by the Conservatives in the committee, in an amendment which was voted down, is the same division that prevails for provincial purposes in that county. Not only have the majority of the committee departed from the division that has existed in the county for the last fifty years, but for some unknown purpose, they have departed-if I am correctly informed-from the division that exists for provincial purposes. And yet we are to imagine, according to the statement of my right hon. friend, that this is done for the purpose of equity, fairness and justice, that there is no sinister motive in it, and that it is absolutely a mere coincidence that a Tory majority of 1,188 votes is hived in one of these extraordinary ridings which have been shown to the Committee to-night t>y the hon. member for Waterloo.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend the leader of the opposition is apparently shocked at' the configuration of the ridings of North and South W'aterioo. But the county of York was divided by the committee on the same principle-so that the urban population within one township might form a separate constituency. If that were placed upon a map, he would find that the configuration would be very much worse than that of the county of Waterloo, but he was not at all shocked at the latter, and if we are to apply motives, no doubt it was because it suited his political friends. My hon. friend must know that very grave difficulties would have arisen if the committee had consented to the division of municipalities, especially of townships, in the rural constituencies. Many applications were made to members of the committee to divide the townships within the ridings, but I would be very sorry to set such a precedent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is the difference between that and going outside the county line ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is a very great difference. My hon. friend sat on the committee two months, and always admitted that he could not understand the province of Ontario, and the more his friends advised him the less he appeared to understand it. No one familiar with the political .conditions of the province of Ontario can fail to know that if the majority on that committee had wished to take political advantage they could without violating any rule, have divided the municipalities in such a way as to cut and carve and make a gerrymander worthy of 1882 if not better than it. We have been challenged from time to time to Show what could have been done. No one knows better than the hon. gentleman who made the challenge, that if we had adopted any such system, we might have gerrymandered to almost an unlimited extent.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I thought that my hon. friend had never investigated those matters.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not know why the hon. gentleman should say that. I do not think he ever found me unacquainted with the conditions of affairs in Ontario. I submit that it would be unfortunate for any party to carve the townships within the county. Why, we had the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram) crying out at the top of liis voice against what he declared to he the most outrageous gerrymander ever perpetrated in any civilized country, and he based that ery solely upon the dividing of townships by the provincial legislature, and in this House a prominent Conservative quoted this very instance, the division of the township of Waterloo, as one of 'the greatest sins ever committed by a provincial legislature. If my hon. friend does not understand, every intelligent elector in Ontario will understand what could have been done if we had undertaken to divide the townships within the counties, so as to gain political advantage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentlemen has repeated two or three times that I said I could not understand the province of Ontario. I never said anything of the kind. I said that I was not as familiar with the divisions of Ontario as my hon. friend, and my hon. friend from Lanark.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
What I said was that the hon. gentleman was not familiar with the conditions in Ontario, and I have come to the conclusion that he does not yet understand the divisions of that province. If he did, he would not advocate the dividing of townships. I would be very much surprised if any of his supporters would want this Bill referred back to the committee in order to have the townships divided. That is one of the reasons why they so bitterly condemned
what they called the Mowat Gerrymander in the county of Waterloo.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And upheld by the hon. gentleman. [DOT]

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
No, I never had anything to do with it. The hon. gentleman is wrong, as usual. We found this system of dividing townships condemned, and condemned with very good reason ; and having refused to divide the townships in other counties we could not divide them in Waterloo, more especially after the dividing of the townships in that county by the Ontario government has been so bitterly condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite.
My hon. friend undertook to say that nothing was done by the majority on the committee except for pure political reasons. Well, I would like to know what motive animated the hon. gentleman's supporters who invited him to put in the proposition he did, and which I was pleased to find he would not move when we came to the constituencies in committee ? What was the motive which induced his followers to make the suggestions they did with regard to the county of Perth ? Was it not to get an unfair political advantage ? And take the counties of Lanark, Huron, Simcoe, Elgin, and even the city of Toronto-

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What about the county of Lanark ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman would only take sufficient interest to read the proposition made in the amendments proposed, I think he would be ashamed of it. It is proposed to separate the township of Sherbrooke from North Lanark and put it into South Lanark.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I proposed to ask the hon. gentleman to consent to that very thing.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman may move that if he wishes, and then he will submit what reasons influenced him other than the most extreme political partisanship.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentlman has no right to charge me with extreme partisanship.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I said that my hon. friend could submit his proposition, and then show if he could name other reasons than a desire to gain a most unfair political advantage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I hope to show very good reasons why the hon. gentleman should consent to it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Well, I have looked into the question, and I think there could not be any fair reason given at all. Speaking for the action of the majority of the committee, I say they were not influenced by those motives more than



they had a right to be. They were not called upon to divide the ridings in such a way as to give their opponents a great advantage, and nobody expected them to do anything of the kind. My hon. friend has condemned this proposition in particular, which is the first one in which he finds, upon information given to him, that he was placing a larger majority of his friends in a constituency than previously existed. As against the one, I can name eight or ten where the propositions placed before us would have the effect of giving his political opponents a much greater advantage than in Waterloo. I am sorry that these charges are made, because they are groundless. I am sorry I have to point out what I think would be the effect of the amendments that were suggested by the opposition members. But, I say the reason given ought to be considered upon their merits, and I think my hon. friend from London has presented them fairly to the House. I think both of the members for Waterloo know that as far as we were concerned there was no intention or desire to interfere with their constituencies in any way. I say that many applications were made, not only to divide townships, but to maintain divisions that now exist for local purposes, and we refused to comply, even when they were made in the instance of our friends. To be consistent I thought it was desirable we should not be placed in the position of having to maintain a division in one county and refusing a similar division in another.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works said there were six or eight amendments moved which would have the result of hiving the Liberals to a greater extent than in the case of Waterloo, or to an equal extent. Will he please begin by naming one ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is one where the result of the division politically would give him a much greater advantage than the placing, as he says, of a majority of Conservatives in this riding, because it would carry two other ridings by the subdivisions he was making. That is the reason it would have a greater political effect. I do not know whether I used the word 'hiving'; I meant that the result of these amendments that he proposed would give his party a greater political advantage that the proposition we have made in the case of Waterloo.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: To justify what the hon. gentleman said a moment ago, he should show one riding in which the Liberals are hived by a majority to the extent of 1,188. I have challenged him to show one of the six or eight and he is unable to do it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I can show' my hon. friend several ridings Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
that are hived to a much greater extent by the Conservative party that by the amendments that we suggested. If I used the words six or eight, I have explained what I meant.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Of course if he meant something else than what he said, we will have to accept it. But there is one observation I would like to make in this connection. A moment ago he said that none of these matters had been considered by him at all, but now he seems to have developed a considerable knowledge of these matters all over the province of Ontario. Might I inquire whether a moment ago he had forgotten that fact ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am surprised that the leader of the opposition would put words in my mouth that I never used. I think he will say at once that he never understood me to say I had no knowledge of these affairs. He asked me how these figures were made up. I am not aware of all the details of this character. If the hon. gentleman will point out where I can find these figures I will look them up.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have no personal knowledge of the figures I gave, they were submitted to me. If they are not correct, I should readily make any necessary acknowledgment. But I certainly think 1 w'as justified in the conclusion that, the hon. gentleman's investigation into this matter had not reached North Waterloo.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think he was. We discussed in committee many of these questions, but I cannot remember every polling division and every township.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works has attempted to give the reasons why a change is proposed in the county of Waterloo. I must say with regard to the reasons advanced by the hon. member for London in the first instance, they did not make a great impression on my mind. It seemed to me that he had entered upon a new field altogether in discussing the reasons why this change should be made, as they were not reasons that were advanced by the committee for former divisions. I think that the Prime Minister, when he comes to consider them, will brush them aside, and deal with the question of Waterloo along the same lines as proposed for other counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman will look at the records of the committee, he will find that he was mistaken. These were the reasons given to the committee.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Not as I understood him, and I have listened carefully to the hon. member for London. Now, the first reason advanced for making

the division as proposed, has existed for fifty years. To my mind, it is a very weak argument, because we would not require to divide a township into two parts. It is already divided ; it has been divided by Act of parliament for 50 years. I have before me the Act of parliament, 16 Victoria, chapter 152. The clause relating to South Waterloo reads as follows :-
The county of Waterloo shall he divided Into two ridings, to be called respectively the North riding and the South riding.
The North riding shall consist of the townships of North Waterloo (including the town of Berlin), Woolwich and Wellesley.
The South riding shall consist of the villages of Galt -and Preston, and the townships of South Waterloo, North Dumfries and Wilmot.
Then follows a description of the township of South Waterloo and a description of the township of North Waterloo.
The present township of Waterloo being divided, for the purposes of representation only, Into tw-Q townships, to be called -respectively the township of North Waterloo and the township of South Waterloo.
Nothing can be plainer to my mind than than that the township is already divided for the purposes for which we are now considering it, into two townships, one called North Waterloo and the other South Waterloo.
The township of North Waterloo -to include and consist of that part of the present township of Waterloo lying within the following limits :
Then it gives the delimitation of the township of North Waterloo, starting at a certain point. The description is somewhat lengthy, and I will not read it all, because we would not be able to follow it without the map before us. It starts at a certain point and runs to another point, ' to the middle of the Grand river, thence along the middle of the said river against the stream ' to a certain other point. After describing thus what should comprise the township of North Waterloo, -the same Act of parliament says:
The township of South Waterloo to include and consist of all ithe remaining part of the said present township of Waterloo.
Now 1 may say this is a very different ease from where we would proceed to divide a township for the purpose of this Bill. This township, I repeat it, and I desire to impress it upon the committee and upon the right hon. leader of the government, was divided for representation purposes fifty years ago past the 14th day of June. It has remained divided for fifty years, not only for Dominion purposes, but for purposes of representation in the local legislature at Toronto. Waterloo is divided in the same way for both Dominion and provincial purposes. Exactly the same definition of North and South Waterloo is given in the Ontario Statute that is given in the chapter from which I have read of the old Act, 16 Victoria, and which has been fol-365J	*
lowed down to the present time-more than half a century. While the hon. Minister of Public Works rejected this division of the township into two townships, and while he condemned the contention of my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) because it perpetuated the divided township, it seems to me that he is willing to accept the division of the county of Brantford, which is divided in a similar way in the same Act of 1853 :
The east riding

-of the county of Brant
-shall consist of the townships of South Dumfries, Onondaga, East Brantford and the village of Baris.
The west riding shall consist of the townships of Bu-rford, Oakland, Tuscar-ora, West Brantford and the town of Brantford.
Here we have East Brantford and West Brantford, and the Act of parliament further says :
The present township of Brantford being divided, for the purposes of -representation only, into the townships of East Brantford and West Brantford : The township of East Brantford to include and consist of all that -portion of the present town-ship of Brantford which lies on the east side of the Gran-d river : And the township of West Brantford -to include and consist of all the remainder of -the present township of Brantford.
Now I would like to know where we are to go to get two cases that are more exactly on a parallel. How are you going to justify the acceptance of Brantford and at the same -time the rejection of Waterloo ? The hon. Minister of. Public Works has drawn a very fine distinction. He says that in one instance the township is divided by the Grand river, and that in the other instance the township is divided only part of the way by the Grand river. I think that is too fine an argument altogether. I do not think the right hon. leader of the government can see any force in that argument. If the fact of a river running all the way through the township of Brantford and dividing it into two parts makes it permissible to divide the township of Brantford, and to put one portion of it into one constituency and another portion into another constituency, surely, when the township of Waterloo is divided by the Grand river a portion of the way and by an ordinary travelled road the rest of the way, no such fine distinction is to be drawn as to say that the argument shall prevail in one case and that it shall be rejected in the other. I leave that in the hands of the right hon. Prime Minister, and I am quite sure he will give it his fair consideration. Now, the other argument used by the Minister of Public Works was that with respect to the piacing of the urban population in one constituency and the rural population in another. He argued that in the case of Waterloo we should have one con-

stituency, including the towns of Berlin, Waterloo, Preston and Hespeler, which contain the greater part of the urban population, and that we should have in addition to that a rural constituency. Granting that there is something in that argument-I am not going to say that it is a fair argument, but if it is a fair argument, why under Heaven is it not a fair argument in the county of Brant ? We offered a resolution to give a representative to the city of Brantford, but hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House declined to accept it They were not then so fond of giving a representative to an urban municipality. No, they opposed it, they spoke against it, and in order to prevent Brantford from exercising its influence as it might exercise it in this parliament as a civic municipality, they insisted that not only a portion of the township of Brantford lying across the river away from the city, but that another township not adjacent to it at all should be added to this urban municipality in order to make up a constituency. But, when we come to Waterloo that is all forgotten, Hon. gentlemen have changed their minds, they have gone back on the principle that they laid down and declared to be right and voted for, and have adopted another principle stating that it is a proper thing that all these civic municipalities, these urban populations should be brought together and constituted into one constituency. I submit this question to the right hon. leader of the government, and I ask him to put the two together and see if he can find the nice distinction which was discovered by the hon. Minister of Public Works. Now, I do not want to say anything about the political complexion of these ridings, because I can hardly for the moment conceive that where a fair redistribution is to be made the right hon. First Minister would consider the political effect of the redistribution. I am not going to say that he would take that into consideration. The fact of the matter is that I do not suppose for one moment that the right hon. gentleman knew anything about what the four members of this committee intended to do until the Bill was actually framed. Of course, now he must deal with it and see whether he regards it as a fair division of the county of Waterloo or not. In regard to the political complexion of Waterloo, let us see whether we can really designate these two ridings as they now stand ns Conservative or Liberal. I think it would be interesting to go back in history. We will take South Waterloo first. In 1867 it was represented by a gentleman who is well known, the Hon. James Young, in 1872 again by the Hon. James Young, by acclamation, and again in 1874 by the same Hon. James Young by acclamation. In 1878, by Mr. Merner, now Senator Merner. He captured the constituency by 44. Then it went Liberal again in 1882 by 208 of a majority,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
when Mr. Livingstone was elected. In 1887 Mr. Livingstone was elected again by 368 majority, in 1891 Mr. Livingstone .again by 312, in 1896, Mr. Livingstone again by 89 majority, and not until 1900 did a Liberal-Conservative represent South Waterloo. Since confederation it was only once represented by a Conservative In this House until the year 1900, when our friend the hon. member who sits behind me (Mr. Clare) succeeded in carrying the constituency. In regard to North Waterloo, it was represented by a Liberal in 1867, when Mr. Bowman was elected by acclamation ; 1872, Mr. Bowman, acclamation ; 1874, Mr. Bowman, acclamation. Then, in 1878 and	in 1882,	it	went	Conservative	bythe	election	of	Mr.	ICranz, but	in
1887 it again returned a Liberal member, when Mr. Bowman carried the seat by 239. In 1891, Mr. Bowman (Liberal) was again elected by 185, and not until 1896 did it again return a Conservative when Mr. Seagram was elected by 309 and in 1900 reelected by acclamation. From confederation down both of these ridings have been represented in this House nearly three-quarters of the time by Liberals, and simply because the people have thought fit to change their political views and to return Conservatives, an attempt is made to change those ridings which have existed for half a century, so that the Conservatives will be hived in one division and the Liberals in the other. I do not say that it is impossible that Waterloo will not send two Conservatives to this House. All things are possible, and I think that nearly everything is possible to our friend (Mr. Clare) who sits behind me, because he went up against a very strong opposition in 1900, and carried the constituency by over 200 majority. Even if his riding is carved out in such a way as to show a majority of 500 or 600 against him, I trust he will be able to overcome that, and come back here after another general election. I would be sorry indeed that this parliament should be deprived of the services of such an able and faithful representative and the people of South Waterloo deprived of the honour of sending Mr. Clare here. For fifty years the hand of parliament has not been laid upon this historic constituency of Waterloo; for fifty years no parliament has dared to drag these people away from their old associations. I trust Sir, that this historic landmark will still remain untouched. I can hardly recall any other county that has remained unchanged so long with two representatives, and I trust that the government will stay its hand and respect the historic rights of the Scotch of South Waterloo and the Germans of North Waterloo. I trust that they will be treated by the parliament of 1903 as they have been treated bv the parliaments of 1853, of 1862, of 1872, of 1882, and of 1892. I trust they may look with confidence to this parlia-

ment to respect their rights as other parliaments have done.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I did not expect to take part in this debate, as I had an opportunity of expressing my views when the constituency I represent was under discussion. I did have sympathy in my heart for the representative of South Waterloo, but that has been to a considerable extent extinguished by the attitude of gentlemen on the other side. When I presented the case of South Brant to this parliament I thought I had a clear case. South Brant had existed for fifty years, but that had no weight with our friends on the other side. The gentlemen who now declare that we should not interfere with the historic arrangement in Waterloo, bad not the slightest hesitation in disrupting the conditions that existed in Brant for fifty years. They expect to gain a political advantage for their side in this case by continuing an arrangement that has lasted for fifty years, but in the case of Brant they expected to gain a political advantage by disrupting a similar historic arrangement. If we could free ourselves from our political environments, we would see that the thing that is right for the county of Brant is not wrong for the county of Waterloo. Why the city of Brantford with
16,000	of a population should have a representative, and the township of Waterloo with 20,000 should not have a representative I do not understand. Why the city of Brantford with 16,000 population should be regarded as an entity, and the township of Waterloo with 27,000 population not regarded as an entity, I do not understand. Our friends on the other side were quite willing to apply to me political extinction if they had a majority in the House, but they are not willing to apply the same principle to Waterloo. If the township of Waterloo has sufficient population to entitle it to a representative, it is a strong reason why township boundaries should not be interfered with. 1 put forward a very reasonable proposition that the county of Brant should be divided into two, by giving Brantford a representative with 19,000 and the county a representative with 18,000, but they thought a political advantage could be gained for their party if they secured a representative for the city of Brantford alone, and so they voted against my proposition. It is to gain a political advantage that they are now moving that the township of Waterloo Shall be divided. In Brantford there is a river running from one end of the county to the other, which affords a natural division, and which has been the dividing line for fifty years, but they were quitte willing to interfere with that. We have heard to-night that South Waterloo is divided by a river for a certain distance. They did not always respect such a boundary. They would not respect it in the case of Brantford. Let me read to you the opinion which was delivered in this House by one of the Conservative leaders, a gentleman in whom our friends opposite have confidence. What did our friend from Victoria say of this very constituency of South Waterloo that is now under discussion ? Herle is what he said when it was in the interest of the Conservative party to find fault with the present arrangemeut:
That the House may properly appreciate how South Waterloo is doctored up and to what extremes these purists of the Liberal party will go to gerrymander a county, I shall read you a description of the county of Waterloo from the Revised Statutes of Ontario, and you will notice that, not content with dividing the municipalities, they even divide lots, and in some places where there is a good old Tory with four or five sons, they draw a line around his lot and hedge him off into another riding in order that he may not do any injury by hie vote to the Reform party.
This was the description of the county from the Act' itself; and these are the words of our friend from Victoria, who was finding fault.	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like to ask who the hon. gentleman means when he says the member for Victoria ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We will call him the member for North Victoria. I have too high an opinion of my hon. friend to assume that he would use such language.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman put what he has read against the Act of parliament ? Which is he going to take-a speech made at random, or an Act of parliament which has existed for fifty years ? I submit that there is no comparison. I gave the Act of parliament, which cannot be questioned. The bon. gentleman has taken an ex-parte statement, perhaps made without any special investigation at the time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Well, I have a very high opinion of my hon. friend who represents North Victoria ; I have a higher opinion of him than my hon. friend from Halton, who wishes to discredit him on this occasion. There is more of that kind in the speech, but I need not quote it any further. Now, what particular injustice is being done to South Waterloo ? I sympathize with the hon. gentleman who represents it ; I regard him as a first-class representative of any municipality ; but my sympathies are not so keen as they were before the Conservative party in this House tried to do exactly what they say we are trying to do to-day ; only they had not justice on their side in trying to divide South Brant and to take out West Brantford without giving Brantford enough population to entitle it to a member. How could a city with 16,000 people expect to have a representative ? In that

respect it differs from South Waterloo, which has 27,000 people, aud which is entitled to a representative on account of its population. Therefore,. in saying that the city of Brantford shouid have added to it Oakland and West Brantford, we were simply equalizing the population so as to qualify Brantford to have a representative. That condition of affairs does not obtain here. North Waterloo will have a population of 25,156 and South Waterloo a population of 27,438. There is no injustice as far as population is concerned. There is no injustice to South Waterloo, because it is entitled to a member because of its population, and also because of the urban character of its people. If an injustice was attempted to be perpetrated, it was when our friends on the other side of the House, who are lifting up their voice against what they call this political iniquity, only a week ago tiled to inflict one on South Brant simply because it would advance their political interest. I have looked over this map, and I see nothing specially wrong in this rearrangement. I would like, of course, to see my old friend come back to this House if he were a Liberal. Unfortunately, however, he is a Conservative ; and, while justice is done, I do not want to see the rewards of justice all an the other side. If hon. gentlemen opposite had manifested a spirit of justice towards us, I would certainly have more sympathy for them. But whenever they have had an opportunity to advance the political interests of their party by suggesting an amendment, that was the whole motive. They did not appear to care what effect it might have on individuals on this side, and I believe the committee were animated in this rearrangement by a sincere desire to do what was right. I believe that if the judges of the land, without knowing the political significance of what is taking place, were asked to divide the county of Waterloo, and were told that Waterloo township had a papulation of 27,000, they would unite in saying that it is entitled to a representative of its own. It is only th'e political significance that is attached to this thing that causes it to be a subject of dispute at the present time. I presume that our friends on the other side would agree that if the political conditions were reversed the divisions should remain exactly as the committee have proposed them. It is just because the political conditions happen to be in favour of the Liberal party that hon. gentlemen opposite are protesting. If it were in the interest of the Conservative party to give the township of Waterloo a member, they would lift up their hands unanimously for it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has twice addressed himself to the discussion of the question, so far as it concerns the county of Waterloo. His second philippic, I think, has been pretty well met by the hon.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd); but with regard to the first, I propose to quote it very briefly, and to say a word or two in repay to it. On page 10855 of the revised ' Hansard ' I read :-
And, Mr. Speaker, you see the result ot this fair measure from ithe map of the county of Waterloo laid on the Table this morning, where a deliberate attempt has been made to hive the Scotch in one section and the Germans in another. What's the matter with the Scotch that their liberties should be taken away?
But how is their seat being taken away by their being hived ? I would rather say that It is a Scotch seat par excellence, and that the Scotch will have a chance of selecting their own representative. If the Germans were in the majority, it is likely they would turn down the Scotchman and elect one of their own race
Why should the Scotch of Galt and Dumfries be hived simply because they are Liberals. It is not necessary to have an election up there at all now-under this Bill we will do the electing for them here. It is the same with the Germans in the north part of that riding. They are told that they are not fit to send a representative to this parliament and that parliament is going to do it for them.
Why ? Because they are put together, they will have the whole say. Is that the reason that they will have no say at all ? I think the same argument applies here. If the Germans are all put in one constituency, they will have all the say, and parliament will have no say at all :
The effect of this measure is simply to have parliament elect two members for the county of Waterloo, one to represent the Germans and another to represent the Scotch, and neither the Seoljish nor the Germans are to have a word to say in the matter, parliament is going to do it for them.
In other words, the Scotch cannot have a word to say, because they are all put in one riding, and the Germans cannot have a word to say because they are all put in one riding. There is another thing to which the hon. gentleman called the attention of the House, which I am satisfied the members of the committee never contemplated, or they would have withheld their sacriligious hands. With reference to the north riding of Waterloo he said :
In the north riding the Germans have a hospital supported by their contributions, and to which they send their islck. That hospital belongs to the north riding of Waterloo, hut to which riding will it belong now ?
Well, Sir, I think we may assume that the people who built and are supporting that hospital will still have the. running of it. and I think we may further assume that it is no fault of this committee that the hospital is involved. That certainly is no reason why we should alter the redistribution made by the committee. One point raised by the hon. the leader of the opposition with regard to the north riding of Waterloo, as constituted under the Act, is a point which has my

sympathy. He says that in that riding there will be a majority of 1,188 Conservatives.
It is certainly a matter for regret that in this twentieth century, this age of educational progress, that any community should be found so ungrateful to the best government that ever administered the affairs of this country as to roll up a majority against it of 1,188. But inasmuch, Sir, as I have a number of Germans in my own riding, of whose intelligence I have learned to form a very high opinion, I am confident that on the next occasion when these people have to express their opinions, we will see an altogether different result.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am glad that the hon. member for Haldimand has gone to the trouble of reading a portion of the speech which I made a short time ago, notwithstanding the fact that in doing so he was breaking one of the rules of the House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What rule ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The rule which prevents quoting from a previous debate.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: But this is the same debate.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I thought it was on a different stage of the Bill. However, I have no objection, and 1 am grateful to the hon. member for having read so much of what I did say, because he has assisted me^ in emphasizing an important point. What I maintain is that the independence of those people in the north and the south ridings of Waterloo, under the new redistribution, is entirely taken away. It will not be necessary to hold an election there except as a matter of form, because in North Waterloo, at any rate, only a representative of one political complexion can possibly be returned. The one riding will be hopelessly Conservative and. the other may be hopelessly Liberal, and no doubt that is what the government contemplated. I am in hopes, however, that the day will arrive when South Waterloo will not be so very far astray, but the odds are very heavy to pit a good man against. I have nothing to take back of what X said. I notice that the hon. gentleman, though a lawyer, did not attempt to deal with the legal phase of the question as to whether there was a township of North Waterloo or a township of South Waterloo. Evidently he is perfectly convinced, and we may consider that, so far as his mind is concerned, that question is settled, and that in the division of Waterloo, as constituted for the past fifty years, there is no contravention of that rule which we all desire to adhere to, when we say a township should not be divided. Under the Act of parliament of 1852-3. the township was divided for all representation purposes into two separate municipalities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I was a little surprised to find the hon. member for Waterloo criticised for thej way in which he presented his case. I thought he had spoken very moderately. Both the hon. gentlemen representing Waterloo have been very mild in anything they have had to say, and at no period have ever used any language to which exception could be taken. When I consider the case of Waterloo I am justified in feeling proud of being a Conservative. In 1891 there were two Liberals representing that county, Messrs. Bowman and Livingstone. During 1882 that county was not interfered with by the cold-blooded Tories who did so much injustice to the Liberal party. In 1891, although there were two Liberals representing Waterloo, the Conservatives did not try to get rid of one of them, but by the redistribution allowed the county to remain as it had been constituted since 1853. According to the census of 1891, there was only a difference of 186 between the two ridings and the Conservative party did not interfere with them, but we have had a marvellous explanation given to-night by the hon. gentleman from London as to why this county has been redistributed in the present Bill. He figures up the different municipalities by reason of certain changes in the population, he explained that this government deemed it of the highest importance to redistribute Waterloo for the purpose of equalizing the population. How are they doing it ? They have done it in such a way that instead of there being a difference of 186 between the two ridings as in 1891, there is now a difference of 2,282. Instead of accepting our proposition, which was to leave the county as it has been divided for fifty years, these hon. gentlemen propose to make a change that will make a greater difference between the two ridings of 624. My hon. friend from London had to go to the county of Brant in order to find a reasonable excuse. What does he say ? He says that there is a river in the county of Brant which makes a natural dividing line, in consequence of which it was necessary to divide the township of Brantford in two. But let us analyse the situation and what do we find ? No doubt the board of trade of the city of Brantford could have suggested a way to avoid the difficulty. What was that way ? They said: The city of Brantford is increasing fast in population. The hon. member for South Brant will not say that the population of Brantford is 16,619 to-day ; it is more like
20,000	to-day. And they, foreseeing the difficulties that will arise if the proposition of my hon. friend from South Brant is carried out, have suggested to my hon. friend and to the government, instead of compelling the people of Brantford township to cross the river, to make the city of Brantford a con-* stitueney. so that the people will not have to go either into or out of the city of Brantford, nor will they be obliged to cross the river.

That is the way they propose to get around the difficulty. But what does the hon. memoir. Heyd) say in reply to the board of trade and the city council ? He says they are not elected to express an opinion on this question.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I used that expression with reference to t|ie city council. The board of trade have a right to express any opinion they like.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Well, we will confine it to the city council. The hon. gentleman says they have no right to express an opinion on this question, because they were not elected on this particular question. Let me remind my hon. friend that the members of the city council have to seek re-election every year by the people of the city of Brantford, while he can sit here for five years without asking the people for approval of his conduct. Let me go further and remind him that we have before us in this House tlie Grand Trunk Pacific question. Was my hon. friend elected on that ? No. Yet he lias the audacity to stand up in this House and express an opinion upon it, without knowing whether that opinion is acceptable to the people or not.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is this difference-I was elected as the representative to come down here and legislate in the interest of this country, not circumscribed in any way. But the city council have their powers circumscribed by an Act of parliament, outside of which they have no power. If they seek to act beyond the limits of the law which creates them, they simply express their opinions as private individuals.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am really sorry for the city councillors or aldiermen of the city of Brantford. The idea of these men having the audacity to suggest an opinion affecting the city of Brantford, whose elected representatives they are ! Whoever heard of so absurd an expression of opinion ? I had thought better of my hon. friend from South Brant than that. Why, the city council have as much right to express an opinion about Brantford as he has-and more, because they are elected yearly, and the people of Brantford look to them to express opinions on matters affecting the welfare of the city. And is it not in accord with common sense to suppose that, recognizing that the city of Brantford is a great manufacturing centre, whose population is likely to increase very fast, and that the views of its citizens are so entirely different from those that may be expressed by the people of Brantford township and Oakland township, a purely agricultural community, they should desire that Brantford should be made a constituency by itself ? Hon. gentlemen opposite take the 3,170 Indians of Tuscarora to equalize the population. And. by the way. that is a familiar name in our politics, I believe it may mean, ' big thunder.' And by

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: that name a famous man from Brant has been popularly known ; and I have heard the voice of little thunder against the redistribution of 1882. I was saying that, in the township of Tuscarora are 3,170 Indians. They have no votes at all. Yet they are counted up in making estimates of population as against the intelligent electors of the city of Brantford. Well, I will suggest a way out of the difficulty. If they want to equalize population, let them take Brantford, with 16,619, and add the figures 3,170 Indians in Tuscarora. That will equalize the population, if that is what is desired, and it will give the city of Brantford an opportunity to vote by itself and will leave the agricultural community of tlie county to vote as they like. But that is not the object. The object of my hon. friend from South Brant, who lives in the city of Brantford, is plain. He is afraid to trust his election to the city of Brantford, because he knows that it is increasing in population, that it is a great manufacturing centre, and: that like other manufacturing centres, its people are not in favour of the policy' of hon. gentlemen opposite, desiring a more decided policy and adequate protection for their industries. My hon. friend is afraid of the people of Brantford, and he wants a riding having a large enough outside vote to defeat the will of the majority in Brantford. Now, here we have the county of Waterloo, which has not been disturbed for fifty years. Who will pretend to say that the electors of that county will not believe that the whole andi sole object of this change is, notwithstanding the modesty of the two gentlemen representing that county, notwithstanding the fact that they have never uttered an offensive word in this House, the whole and sole object is to wipe out one of these gentlemen in order to secure the election of a supporter of the government. Yet hon. gentlemen on the other side will stand up in their places in this House and say that this is a modest redistribution, it is a redistribution which is thoroughly justified and that ought to be adopted in this House.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I suppose that, by this time, we might come to some conclusion of this debate. But, before I proceed further, I may say to my hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) that no fault can be found, assuredly, with the way which my hon. friend from South Waterloo (Mr. Clare) presented his case. He presented his view in very moderate and temperate language ; and even those who are not disposed to agree with him in everything, could not find fault with bis manner of laying his view before the committee. My hon. friend from South Waterloo thinks that he would be injured by the redistribution now contemplated'. He made a strong point of the fact that the constituency he represents has been in existence for fifty years

or thereabouts. Ou the other hand, I cannot admit that the redistribution that is proposed is outrageous, which is the adjective by which some hon. gentlemen opposite have described it. It proposes to place
27,000	of a population in one riding and about the same number in another riding. Perhaps this new arrangement would be warranted by the fact that the population in the county of Waterloo has changed very much, and that in the township of Waterloo itself there is now' a population of 25,000 or thereabouts. But, as against this, for my part, I do not pretend to treat lightly the objection made by my hon. friend that there is, even in the face of that, no substantial reason wrby the arrangement that exists should be altered in any way. Perhaps, under the circumstances, it would not be inadvisable that we should give the matter more thought, and, for that purpose, the item should stand.
Item 50 allowed to stand.
On item 52-the county of York,

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I would like the Chairman of the committee to tell me exactly w'hat principle has been guiding the committee respecting the apportionment of members to the county of York? The population of the county of York, if my memory serves me, at the last distribution was about 90,000. York was given three members, the unit of representation being about 30,000. The basis explains everything. If they were previously for electoral purposes in
the county of York, they wrere part of the municipal city of Toronto. Is not that right ?

speechtext: I have explained to the committee that we dealt with the city of Toronto arbitrarily, as we did with the city of Montreal.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We had it under consideration. We have had ridings and counties in the province of Ontario under consideration in which no change has been made, Now the hon. gentleman asks me how the county of York is dealt with. After separating the city of Toronto it was divided into three constituencies. The population I think is fairly equally divided, at least I have heard no complaints that any political advantage has been taken. As a member of the committee I have been told by many people that we did a great injustice to the Liberal party, and there was no reason why a fair division could not have been made which would change the political complexion very materially. So if my hon. friend has been able to point to one or two cases in which he thinks that the majority of the committee took some advantages for political purposes, he 'will be able to say that in the county of York at least the Liberals on the committee did not take the advantage they might have taken for partisan purposes. I do not know of any other reason to give of the way the county of York has been treated. The city of Toronto was considered separately, as different from all the other municipalities in the province, and then the county of York was divided according to the same rule that applied to all other counties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman asked me to show him wherein there has been any political advantage gained by the Liberals in the distribution of the county of York. I am sorry that the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) is not here to-night, because probably he is in a better position to explain the situation in the county than I am.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. member for York was before the committee, and I have not heard any complaint from him.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I find some statements in the Toronto ' News,' an ardent supporter of the Bill, which I propose to read, and if there is anything wrong in these figures the minister will correct me, I hope :
York Centre, new constituency-Gains Markham township and village and Scarborough township with a Liberal majority of 270, gains Vaughan, Etobicoke, Richmond Hill, Weston and Woodbridge with a Liberal majority of 33.

That makes a Liberal majority in York Centre of 303.	'
York, East-W. F. Maclean-His majority of 642 is abolished.
York, North, represented by the Postmaster General, gains Whitchurch and the townships of Newmarket and Stouftville with 217 Liberals majority ; and loses Gwillimbury and the township of Bradford with 31 Conservative majority. That constituency given a Liberal majority of 545.
York, South, new constituency, gains East. Toronto town with a Conservative majority of SO ; sains Toronto junction, township of York and North Toronto village with a Conservative majority of 281. Gains York township in East York with a Conservative majority of 365. That is a Conservative majority altogether of 726.
All of West York has been abolished.
Tlie figures in the ' News ' show that at. the last general election there was a Conservative majority in West York of 820, and that has been decimated if not destroyed by the redistribution of the county of York. But the hon. gentleman can hardly say that if these people had remained in the county of York they would have been disfranchised. They are practically disfranchised by being brought into the city of Toronto ; because, while it is true, as the Prime Minister has said,' that Toronto is receiving an additional member, lie must not overlook the fact that a population equal to nearly three times the unit of representation in this House has been added to the population of the city. I want to know upon what principle the unit in the county of York has been reduced' to 21,000, while in Toronto it has been increased from 36,000 to 42,000?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
In reference to the county of York, the arrangement that was come to by confining the constituencies to county boundaries, of course sets the city of Toronto off by itself, and places the county of York by itself. The population of the county of York is sufficient to entitle it to three members, and it has been divided, so that the population of the three constituencies is almost equal. I do not see how any objection can be taken to the division of the county of York. With regard to Toronto, the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) says that the unit of population is largely Increased; in other words, 64,000 people have been added to the city of Toronto and only one more member has been given to it. Now the hon. member forgets that when the census was taken in 1891 the population of the city of Toronto was
181,000	; in 1901 it was 208,000. To get a fair comparison, you will have to take East and West York and all of the city, because in the city, as I say, there were 181,000 people according to the census of 1891.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That is including the part of Toronto in East and West York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Certainly. Under that arrangement there were about 37,000 p eople Mr. CLARKE.
of the city of Toronto found in East and West York, leaving 144,000 in the city of Toronto proper, which was awarded four members. By putting those 37,000 people in East and West York they were practically disfranchia(ed because there was enough population in East and West York to have entitled them to two members. West York was set off with 41,000 people and East York with 35,000 people. Let us take the city of Toronto. Under the redistribution of 1892 there was Toronto Centre with
26.000	and East Toronto with 43,565. That was equalizing the population. Twenty-six men in Centre Toronto were just as good as forty-three and a half in East Toronto. Then in West Toronto there were 73,862 persons for two members. If we take East and West York, because we have to take them into consideration as they embraced a part of the city of Toronto, we find that West York had a population of 41,857 and East York a population of 35,148 making a total of 221,064 persons to whom there were allowed six members, or am average of 30,866 persons to a member. Under this redistribution we have the city of Toronto with 208,000 people, York Centre with 21,507 people, and York South with 20,699 or a total of 250,246 people. This territory comprises exactly the same territory as was dealt with by the redistribution of 1892 and to these 250,246 people we are now granting seven members or a member to 35,700 people against the old apportionment of a member to 30,800 people. The committee will therefore see that under the present redistribution the city of Toronto, embracing Centre and South York, is given a member for every
1.000	people less than was allowed under the Redistribution Act of 1892. For the city of Toronto with the 181,000 people that it had in 1891 there were only four members awarded or a member for 45,303 persons.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman says that the city of Toronto had only four members for 181,000 people. He must also include in that the fact that West York and East York had a very large representation.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It is true that 37,000 people living in Toronto Were shoved into the ridings of East and West York and that they were practically disfranchised because East and West York had enough people to give them two members without this addition of population from the city of Toronto at all. In that way hon. gentlemen opposite brought up the unit of representation to 36.000. They shoved off 37,000 people into the adjoining ridings and left 144,000 people in the city of Toronto and gave four members to these 144,000 people allowing on e member to every 36,000 of a population. and East York because these ridings, as I have said, had sufficient population to entitle them to two members.
