maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It strikes me that the Iron, member for West York (Mr. Campbell) created a wrong impression because he made a statement which is not susceptible of proof. I would he sorry to think that he made that statement intentionally, but he said that the population of Toronto in 1891 was 181,000. Those were the figures that he mentioned. I took them down.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have the census.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman in making that statement forgot, or overlooked or ignored the fact that he was including in that 181,000 the 37,000 people living in territory that was never Included m the city of Toronto for the purposes of the representation of that city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Campbell) explained that at the time.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
No, the hon. gentleman did not explain it. He went on to state that the unit of representation in the city of Toronto, in being giveu four members for a population of 181,000, was something over
45.000	for each member, while the fact is that the population of Toronto as shown in the census returns of 1891 was 144,000. and that being given four members it had a unit of 36,000. The county of York at the same time had a population of 97,000, and it was given three members or a unit of about
32.000	for each. I am asking information now, and I desire to know on what principle, or for what reason, the unit of representation for Toronto has been increased to 42.000, while for York the unit has been reduced to 21,000 ? The minister has not attempted to explain that. The population of York has been reduced now to 64,000 odd, and yet the number of members remains at three, while the population 0f Toronto under this Bill is increased from 144,000 to 208,000, an increase of 64,000, and it is only given one additional member, York has been decreased 30,000 and it retains three members; Toronto has

been increased 61,000 and it gets one additional member. What principle of justice, or fair play, or honesty is there in a redistribution of that kind ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Is there any rhyme' or reason why 37,000 citizens of Toronto should be placed in the constituency of York ? Is there any reason why West York should have a population of over 41,000, 20,000 of whom are in the municipality of Toronto, and that East York should have 36,000, 15,000 of whom belong to Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There is very great reason why that should be. The contention of the government is, that large centres of population should have fewer representatives than the rural constituencies. I do not believe in that. As a matter of fact one of these Yorks has an urban population now, and when the next census comes around, that population will be practically a city population. The population will overflow from Toronto and increase the surrounding suburbs. That is a reason why the adjoining constituencies of York should to some extent have the same proportionate representation as the city of Toronto. The unit of representation in the three Yorks, instead of being up to the general unit of 24,381, is as a matter of fact only 21,541. If there is any reason in the contention of the government, that the dense population of the city should have smaller representation than sparsely settled counties, that reason is just as strong why the thickly populated districts adjoining Toronto, whose population is in a measure an overflow from Toronto, should have a larger unit for representation than the average country constituency. Instead of that being carried out in the case of the three Yorks, their unit of representation is 3,000 less than the average of the country constituencies, and 20,000 less than in the city of Toronto. I say that the county of York, with 60,000 inhabitants, 20,000 of whom are tributary to Toronto, should not have more than two members if Toronto is to be cut down to five. I say that two members are more in proportion for the county of York than five members are for the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) takes a very narrow view of this great question of redistribution for the province of Ontario. If he had appeared before the committee and suggested that the county of York has too many representatives, I dare say we would have been pleased to have taken that into consideration.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: He did not say that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If that is not his argument, I do not know what it is. We had to have one general rule governing the province, and the county of York was entitled to three members under that rule.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Our objection is that you have not one general rule governing the province.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Have I got to say every time that Toronto is an exception ?	1 thought that was well
known by this. These inequalities of population must exist. The majority of the committee held that the urban population was not entitled to the same consideration as the rural population, and that has been recognized in this country ever since confederation, and it is recognized in other countries as well. When Sir John Macdonald was Prime Minister of Canada he adhered to that rule, and my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) thought it was all right. We never heard any protest from him then.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When Sir John Macdonald was Prime Minister.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My dear man, I was not born in politics then.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: That will explain a great many of the peculiar actions of my hon. friend (Mr. Osier) now. He is so very young that he does a lot of these things for want of knowledge. But when the hon. gentleman attempts to discuss these questions he ought to know something at least of the history of his own party in Canada, and the custom of both parties in England.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Wrhat does my hon. friend say is the rule in England ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have discussed that frequently with the leader of the opposition, and he knows it very well.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman say there is any difference in the unit if you take the whole borough constituencies, and the whole of the rural constituencies in England ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
When my hon. friend talks about boroughs, that is 'merely a catch question. You might as well ask us why we don't equalize population in West Northumberland or Prince Edward, or in some of these smaller counties. AVhat does the hon. gentleman mean by rule ? He says that because there is some small borough iu England which has been allowed to exist for some time, that justifies a larger representation for the urban population as compared with the rural population. But coming back to Canada, when we were losing six representatives from the province of Ontario, I would have been inclined to suppose that the people of Toronto and the members for Toronto would have given a majority of the committee credit for dealing fairly with the city under the circumstances, when we

might have given to one of the counties the additional member who was given to the city, if he wished to act, as some bon. gentlemen opposite assert we have done, for party purposes, and we could easily have justified our action. It is because it appealed to our sense of justice, on account of the growth of the city, that we decided to recommend it a larger representation, even though the province was losing six members. -Yet my hon. friend does not seem to be satisfied. I think that the rest of the province of Ontario will feel that the committee could not fairly have gone further than they did in that respect. Many of the rural constituencies will no doubt feel that we were very liberal to the city of Toronto in giving it an additional member, if there were no better reasons than the gentleman has given to-night. If, according to the hon. gentleman's argument, the city of Toronto were to be given a representation on the same unit as the rest of the province, it would have say four additional members ; and if so, four members would have to be taken from some of the rural counties. I do not think he has advanced any good reason why that should be done ; but, on the contrary, I think the conclusion we have come to is the right one. Some of the rural constituencies are represented in this House by men who live in cities. They are centres of financial and general commercial influence throughout the country. Their people know what is going on, and they make their views known to parliament much more easily than the people of the rural constituencies. Many reasons of that kind make it reasonable to give the rural districts a larger representation than the cities.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I think it is a poor argument against increasing the representation of the city to say that a member representing a rural constituency resides in the city. In my experience in this House, I have not noticed that the two or three gentlemen who represent rural constituencies and reside in Toronto, have taken any interest in Toronto affairs. Their interest is concentrated in their own ridings.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have often seen members who represent the city of Toronto acting very much against the interests of the city. That is only a matter of opinion.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The Minister of Public Works has never lived in a large city, and does not understand what is necessary.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We farmers have to learn, you know.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman had lived in a large city like Toronto for some time, he might know what is necessary in a city of that size. I wish to draw attention to the fact that Toronto is not going to be as well represented in the future, so
far as number is concerned, as it lias been in the past.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We may improve the quality.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In the past Toronto lias practically had six representatives in this House. The hon. member for West York has represented a city population of 52,757, according to the census ; that is a greater population than that of any of the constituencies which are proposed by the county of York, where the largest number is 22,419.	.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman compared the urban population in what is now South York with what was in West York previously ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: No, I have not the figures.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have not either, but I know that there is a larger urban population in South York than there was in West York before.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The member for East York has represented a city population of 20,666, according to the last census. This is made up as follows : In Ward 1, 10,465 ; in Ward 2, 3,138 ; in Ward 3, 7,063. The city population in West York; is made up as -follows : In Ward 6, 21,296 ; in Ward, 5, 4,338 ; in Ward 3, 123. The smallest number in any of the rural constituencies in the county of York is 20,699, being only three more than the city population which is represented by the hon. member for East York at the present time. So, I do not think it can be disputed that Toronto in the past has enjoyed in this House a representation of six members, and that is now going to be practically reduced to five members. I do not quite understand why Toronto has been allotted only five members. If there is anything in the argument put forth by the hon. Minister of Public Works, surely the government are going to the very extreme in dividing Toronto in the way they have done, and only giving it five members. Toronto Centre is to have a population of 43,861, Toronto East 40,097, Toronto North 40,983, Toronto South 38,108, and Toronto West 44,991. It makes one feel rather sad to see what is being done in other cities and constituencies in Ontario. The city of Brantford will have a population of 19,687, Kingston 19,788, Hamilton East 24,000, and Hamilton West 28,634. How the majority of the committee arrived at the decision that Toronto should only have five members is something I cannot understand. There is no doubt that Toronto should be represented^ by six members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The population of Toronto in 1891, constituted for representation in this House, was 144,023. That gave four members, or 36,000 for each member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The whole city was 181,000.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is confounding two entirely different things. Toronto had 144,000, and it had four members. The county of York had three members representing 97,000. What we want to know is why the unit of representation of Toronto has been increased from 36,000 to 41,608 ? The additional 04,000 is practically getting only one representative. The county of York has a population of 64,000, and is given three representatives. But the addition to the population of Toronto of
64,000	secures only one representative. Upon . what principle of justice and fair-play is this done ? It is'not fair to assert that the population of Toronto is 181,000 unless you also explain that that population included the wards of St. Alban, St. Mark, St. Paul and St. Matthew, which were never in Toronto for the purposes of representation until the present Bill. The population of those wards amounted to about 37,000. But the Minister of Public Works says lie has done us justice in giving us an additional member, andi that the feeling was against our getting an additional member. Surely we are being discriminated against sufficiently when our unit is 41,608 against 24,381 for the rest of the province. The argument has been used that in years gone by the leader of the Conservative party favoured giving urban constituencies less representation than the rural, but hon. gentlemen opposite are quoting from a statesman who is dead, and whom, during his lifetime, they never ceased to attack. But I would line to draw attention to the fact that there is a new departure being taken now. We were to have followed the English precedent, laid down in 1884-5 by Mr. Gladstone. That, I understand, was the basis ou which this Bill was to be carried through. It is not being carried through on that basis, because the discrimination against the urban population, so far as regards Toronto, is much greater than the discrimination against the urban population in the United Kingdom. My hon. friend from East Toronto made reference to the population of other cities of Ontario, and showed that the rule applied to Toronto had not been applied to them. They have a population in the aggregate of 190,193, and they will haw seven representatives in this House. Kingston, Brantford and London have each one, and Hamilton and Ottawa have each two. Our population in Toronto is greater by 18,000 than the entire population of all these cities, and yet we have only five members while they have seven mem-besrs. Surely that is gross discrimination.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What would be the remedy ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Apply the rule which Mr. Gladstone applied to England. The right hon. gentleman, when introducing this measure, spoke as follows :
The last redistribution which took place in England took place in 1884, under .the government of Mr. Gladstone. On that occasion, Mr. Gladstone, before making his Bill, adopted the policy which we intend to follow on this occasion. The Bill was prepared, at the invitatiou of Mr. Gladstone, by a conference of the two parties in the House of Commons, by a conference of the government and the opposition. Mr. Gladstone invited Lord Salisbury, who- was then the leader of the opposition, ito meet with , him and discuss with him the details of the Redistribution Bill which he had to introduce, following consequent upon the new Franchise Acit. This .conference took place, and, as a result a measure was introduced which proved satisfactory to both parties.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is the principle my hon. friend is advocating-that Toronto should have increased representation? What is the remedy he proposes?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If I undertook to introduce a scheme of redistribution, I would assume the responsibility.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend cannot give more than 86 members to Ontario. If he gives ten to Toronto, be must take five from somewhere else.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The right bon. gentleman would surely not expect a bumble member of tbe opposition to re-draft the whole scheme of the representation of Ontario. He is the guardian of the rights of the people, and what we are contending for is that a gross injustice shall not be done to one section of the people of Ontario, and we appeal to him to rectify what we believe to be a grievous wrong.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is tbe principle on which Mr. Gladstone acted with reference to population ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Let me quote a few paragraphs from Anson's Law and Custom of the Constitution.'

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have Mr. Gladstone's speech on introducing his Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I have read his speech, and will take the liberty of quoting some sentences from it. This is what Anson says:
The Redistribution Act of 1885 differs from its predecessors in that it departs to a great extent from the principle of local representation. and Is professedly based on an attempt to divide the members equally, or with a rough attempt at equality, among the population.
So, this was a new departure, and a departure in tbe direction of representation by population. Then the next paragraph points out the anomaly that existed prior to 1885 :
Before the Act became law the average throughout the country of population to members was. in counties, 78,000, in boroughs, 41.200. to a member. But this proportion was not preserved : for instance, 79 boroughs in England, with pomilations under 15,000, each returned a

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
member, and 36 boroughs, with populations under 50,000, each returned two members.
The Redistribution Act starts on the principle, sacrificed to some extent in favour of local representation, that the proportion of 54.000 to a member should be the basis of calculation. All towns with a population of less than 15,000 are thrown into their respective counties, whether or no they have previously returned members. Towns which have more than 15.000 inhabitants and less than 50,000 are to return one member ; those which have more than 50,000 and less than 165,000 are to return two members ; and beyond this an additional member is given for every additional 50,000 of population ; and the county representation is based in like manner upon numbers.
If hon. gentlemen opposite will apply to tlie city of Toronto the rule which Anson lays down here, taking the unit for the whole province, they will find that the city of Toronto would be given seven members under the proposition of Mr. Gladstone, instead of five members as under the proposition of the right hon. gentleman (Rt. non. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). To show what was proposed under that Redistribution Act, let me quote a few paragraphs from the speech of the Right Hon. Mr. Gladstone. They had difficulties to overcome that do not present themselves here, though there are difficulties in every redistribution measure, Some were thus described :
They were obliged to have regard to ancient divisions of counties and to old historic parliamentary representations of municipalities. The House had to pay some respect to ancient arrangements and ancient rights.
But they acted upon this principle :
To apply to the electoral areas of the country one and the same rule throughout.
The electoral areas will he dealt with as units, and with an unvarying equality of principle of treatment.
That is all that we are asking should be done so far as the city of Toronto is concerned under the Bill that we are now discussing. Under the Bill of 1885, the metropolitan district of London was given 37 additional members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What was the population ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I will give the hon. gentleman the population. Liverpool was given six additional members ; Birmingham, four additional members ; Manchester, three additional members ; Sheffield, three additional members ; Leeds, two additional mem' hers. Now, let me take ten of the principal cities and towns and show the relation of their representation of population :

Take the combined population of these ten cities and towns, and the combined representation, and apply the rule that I have quoted from Anson, and you will find that the unit is practically observed throughout the whole list. The unit of population for London is between 63,000 and 64,000. And, if you take these ten leading cities and towns in England and Wales and apply the rule I have quoted, you will find there is no discrimination against them because they are urban constituencies. The argument that we have been urging to the best of our ability upon the right hon. gentleman is that there is nothing in the Gladstone Redistribution Act, there is no principle affirmed or laid down in that Act, that justifies the discrimination, the unique discrimination, the 'arbitrary discrimination, which he is practicing in this Redistribution Bill. If there was discrimination against other cities of Ontario, there would be some; argument for applying it to Toronto. But it does not apply. I have given the figures and need not elaborate them now.
There is another point in which this Redistribution Bill differs radically, in a most essential feature and principle, from that of the late Mr. Gladstone. It is a comparatively easy matter to agree as to a constituency entitled to one member. But when he came to deal with constituencies entitled to two or more members, it was of the very essence of the agreement between Gladstone and Salisbury that in the delimitation of the boundaries of the several constituencies, absolute justice and fair-play should be meted out. And, for that reason, before Mr. Gladstone introduced his measure in the House of Commons, he announced that a boundary commission had been appointed, and he named that commission. The commission was composed of men not engaged in the active pursuit of politics, hut rather professional men, engineers and surveyors. And the instructions which he gave to these commissioners were brought down to the House. And what were those instructions ? I quote a part:
In the first place to examine 'the survey maps of the Ordnance Department and determine from them and other documents in the possession of that department and of the local government hoard, and from other available information, 'the boundaries to be assigned to the several divisions of each county to be divided. In forming the divisions the population of the several divisions, excluding that of the parliamentary boroughs, should 'be equalized so far as practicable, and care must be taken in all those cases where there are populous localities of an urban character 'to include them in one and the same division, unless this cannot he done without producing grave inconvenience and involving boundaries of a very irregular and * objectionable character.
Subject to this important rule, eacli division should be as compact as possible with respect to geographical position, and should be based upon well-known existing areas, such as petty sessional divisions, or other areas consisting of an aggregate of parishes. In some instances,

however, it may be found necessary to include separate parishes, but a divisional boundary must never be allowed to intercept a parish.
There is another paragraph, and one to which I would draw the attention of the right lion. Prime Minister :
When the divisions have thus been provisionally determined, public notice must be given of their contents by advertisement in one or more local newspapers, a day and place appointed for the attendance of one of the members of the commission at some principal town in the county to hear any objections to tho proposed constitution of the divisions and receive proposals for their alteration.
So, when the redistribution was about to take place, the principles to govern the representation in the parliament of Great Britain were laid down and agreed to between the parties, before the measure was introduced at all, and a boundary commission was appointed to act independently of either the House of Commons or its committees, and solely upon the instructions which were given to the commissioners. It was impossible to have a fairer measure than that proposed by Mr. Gladstone. But in essential features the measure which the right hou. gentleman took as his model has been departed from in the measure now before us. Just imagine, if you can, the boundary commission sending out draft diagrams of the Greys, or the Middlesexes, or Waterloos, or of any of these constituencies that have been up for consideration to-'day, and illustrated before this Committee. What reception would they meet with from the people ? In Mr. Gladstone's redistribution Bill, the residents of the constituencies to be delimited by the boundary commission were given an opportunity of seeing what the commission proposed to do, and presenting their views against any proposed delimitation of the commissioners. Surely I need not pursue that any further than to point out that according to the statements that have been made here during the past week, when the committee were delimiting the boundaries of the constituencies in counties where there was more than one member to be returned, almost every suggestion that emanated from the minority of that committee as to a modification of the delimitation agreed upon by the majority, was rejected without any consideration. I myself and my colleagues went before the committee to make a protest against the way Toronto was being treated ; but, of course, we had nothing but cold, dull ears turned towards us. That is the reason why we have to take up so much time from day to day in presenting our case before the committee.
The case of Montreal is brought up. The right hon. gentleman tells us that wnen we are dealing with one constituency we ought to deal with that and not with another. But the argument has been protruded that Montreal is treated like Toronto. Now,
the franchise in Quebec is different from that in Ontario. We have practically one franchise, one man one vote. If that is a sound principle, surely the people who, in great urban constituencies like Toronto, have a keener struggle for existence, who have to lead a more strenuous life to make a living, surely when they are hived together in a great constituency where there are so many divergent political views and opinions, it is in the highest degree essential that they should have the same chance of being represented upon the floor of parliament. Why should these peoples' votes be discriminated against because they reside in a great urban municipality ? If the unit is 24,381 outside the city of Toronto, and each man in Ontario has only one vote, why should not that same unit apply to the city of Toronto so that those entitled to vote in Toronto may have an equal influence with those who are more fortunate in living outside the city ?
The right hon. gentleman has argued again and again that justice should be done to the outlying and sparsely settled parts of the province. Let me give him a few figures. The urban constituencies of Ontario, the population of the cities other than Toronto, which will have representation in this parliament are : Kingston, 19,788 ; Brantford, 19,867 ; London, 37,976 ; Hamilton, 52,634 ; Ottawa, 59,928. These in the aggregate amount to 190,193, giving a unit of representation of 27,170. But when you come to examine the outlying parts of the province, these great sparsely settled areas have a larger unit of population. While the cities other than Toronto have a unit of 27,170, these sparsely settled districts have a unit of 27,216. If the urban constituencies are not entitled to as much representation as the outlying and sparsely settled districts, upon what principle have these cities been given a representation based on the unit of 27,170, while the outlying sparsely settled parts of the province are only accorded a unit of representation of 27,216 ? Let me point out further that in these outlying districts the population is steadily increasing. During the last ten years it has increased by about twenty-five per cent. These are progressive communities, they are on the frontier of civilization, and great strides are being made by them. Yet in apportioning them their representation in this parliament that fact has not been taken into consideration, and I will prove the fact. If you take the older counties of the province of Ontario, the metropolitan counties, you will find that Northumberland, Prince Edward, Brant, Middlesex, Huron, West Elgin, Lanark and York, have a population of 325,856, and they will have seventeen members on the floor of parliament ; while these outlying constituencies to which I have referred, having a population of 326.476, will have only twelve members to represent them. Upon what

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: principle of representation is this redistribution being carried out ? To my mind it is most unfair and unjust, if we accept the principle laid down by the Prime Minister, that urban constituencies are not entitled to as much representation in proportion to population as rural ; or, if we take the other argument, that these outlying districts are entitled to a smaller unit of population than the older and more fully settled districts of the province. Now, I appeal to the principles laid down by Mr. Gladstone in his Redistribution Act of 1885, and to the Prime Minister's language in introducing this Bill, and I ask that justice be done to the great urban municipality of which I have the honour of being one of the representatives. It is not an unreasonable request to make, it is a request based upon justice and fair-play and for an equality in the value of votes. I appeal to the right hou. gentleman, if he desires that these principles shall prevail, that he will not turn a deaf ear any longer to the fair and reasonable proposition that this one municipality, having one-tenth of the population of the province, should not be treated so unfairly and harshly as is being done in this proposed Bill.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The argument which my bon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has presented to us is not new. With respect to the comparison which he has made between urban and rural populations, I must still maintain the ground which-I took, even after the argument he has presented to us. I say it is impossible under our constitution to give the same representation to the urban population as to the rural population. Now, my bon. friend must keep this in mind : In England, when Mr. Gladstone made his distribution, he was not limited in the number of representatives. I do not know the exact number of representatives in the English House of Commons at the present time, it is between 500 and 600, but it might be 700 or 800. In our case, the province of Ontario is limited to eighty-six members. You cannot get away from this fact, that if you apply the same rule to the urban as to tbe rural population, and if the unit is to be maintained of 25,000 the city of Toronto would be entitled to some ten members, and you would have to wipe out five rural constituencies. There is no government that would do that. Eet my hon. friend also take heed to Mr. Gladstone's opinion when he said that we must keep in mind old constituencies, we must have consideration for historical traditions. Now, would it l>e possible to wipe out any of the existing constituencies ? Would it be possible to wipe out any of the counties ? Why, my hon. friend must know that three-fourths of all the time we have taken up in debate during the last four days, has been by members who were to lose some 366
constituencies now in existence, and who were protesting against it. These are the reasons which make it impossible in my view to give the same representation to the urban as to the rural population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I would draw attention to the fact that by the reduction in the county of York from three to two, the unit of representation would be 32,312 as agaiust 41,608 in the city of Toronto.
The PRIME MINISTER No, that argument does not hold because the county of York to-day is limited to the rural portion, whereas before it had a mixed community containing both an urban and a rural population.

speechtext: I assumed the population was 250,000.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: If the theory of my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) is carried out it will only be eight members and not ten. That wuuld be three members more. I would like to know how the committee arrived at the decision that Toronto should only have five members, since the city of Toronto in the past has been represented by six members. If exception is taken to the statement that Toronto has in the past had six members by counting the two hon. gentlemen who represent East and West York surely hon. gentlemen opposite cannot say that Toronto has not been represented by five members, because we are certainly entitled to count these two hon. gentlemen as being equivalent to oue member.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Will not South York, as it is proposed to be constituted in this Bill, include a considerable number of the urban population? South York practically includes the suburbs of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They are uot in the city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Even if that division does not represent the city of Toronto you only have a unit of 20,000 odd.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. member for East York represents a population of 20,666 and and the hon. member for West York a population of 25,757 in the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: A rural population.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Making a total population represented by these two gentlemen of 46,423. If we count these two as one we will have Toronto represented by five members instead of six. I am sure that these two hon. gentlemen have felt that they had an interest in the affairs of Toronto, and they have felt that they were representatives of



Toronto, probably not to as great an extent as those of us who represent purely city constituencies, but you may consider the two of them as one, and Toronto therefore in the past has had five representatives. Notwithstanding the increase in population, Toronto is still to have five members. I would like to ask on what principle the committee arrived at the decision to give Toronto five members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: They did it arbitrarily.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I am sure there was something at the back of it. Did they take into consideration the fact that Toronto has had six members in the past, or if not six that it lias had five in the past, counting the two members for East and West York as one ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Kemp) argued a little while ago that the members representing constituencies outside of the city, although representing an urban population, did not take much interest in the city and he said that because previously the two members for East and West York had a considerable urban population they were considered as city members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did. not say that.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Toronto has six members now because the constituency of South York is practically an urban constituency; in fact, it is altogether so, except that a small portion of the township of York which is occupied by inhabitants who are engaging in farming. Now, my hon. friend asks why the com-, mittee did not give an extra member to Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Oh, no, my question was this : On what rule or basis was the decision arrived at to give five members to the city of Toronto? What discussion was there by the committee which resulted in giving five representatives to Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The city of Toronto had four members representing it in this parliament before. My hon. friend claims that it had six.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And you give it five now.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
That is the argument. He asks the question :	How is it ? In the first place, the
hon. gentleman knows that we returned to the principle of adopting municipal boundaries. The city of Toronto was then considered as a separate municipality. It was treated arbitrarily. The question was then as to whether it should have any more representatives than it had previously. The province was losing six members. It was < thought by a majority of the committee that Toronto might still be entitled to one member. There had to be a reduction in other parts of the province. We also thought it well that increased representation Mr. KEMP.
should be given to the growing districts in the northern part of the province.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: You did not do that. You made the unit of representation in the northern parts of the province higher than it is in the other parts of the province.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We gave the northern part of the province three extra members.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And made the unit higher.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We took the conditions as they were. It has been pointed out so often, and I think it is a good and sufficient argument, that it it was impossible for the committee to apply any mathematical rule. Has any hon. member even attempted to suggest any rule that could be applied that would work out more satisfactorily than this has done ? I think the hon. gentleman must see the difficulty that the members of the committee have to contend with in view of the fact that they were limited to municipal county boundaries. We thought it was proper and right that the city of Toronto should have one more representative.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: One less.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: One more. I am not joking with my hon. friend at all. I say we did allow one more to the municipality of Toronto and in dividing the county of York instead of breaking the county boundaries and adding to the population that might really belong as an urban population to Toronto and allowing six members we endeavoured as nearly as possible to give the urban population of the city six representatives.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works is apparently under the impression that a part of the constituency of South York is virtually within the city limits. That is not the case. As I have said 46,423 of the population of the city of Toronto have been represented by the hon. meiuber for West York and the hon. member for East York.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: What is the total population of East York and West York ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I have not the figures.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: 51,000 for West York by the last census.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: By any stretch of imagination can any hon. gentleman say that Toronto has not had at least five representatives in the past within the city limits counting the two representatives of East and West York as one ? Therefore, the representation of the city of Toronto has not been increased in any sense.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
I want to say a few words in regard to the position of the committee

when it came to deal with the representation of York and Toronto ? In the first place we all know that the number of members in the province of Ontario had to be reduced from 92 to 86 which meant a loss of six members. In addition to that it was incumbent upon us owing to the increased population in the outlying districts of Ontario to give three members to these districts. The committee therefore found that so far as the old constituencies in Ontario are concerned, they had to deal practically with a loss of nine seats. The total population of York is 272,763, of which the city of Toronto constitutes 208,040 and the township of York 64,623. The county of York was dealt with exactly the same as all the other counties. When it came to Toronto we had before us the manner in which the cities of Toronto and Montreal had been dealt with in the previous redistribution. It seems to me that instead of our having to defend ourselves for following the methods adopted in 1881 and 1891, the burden of proof is on the other side of the House to show why we should change.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We gave you the reasons.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: And I hope to show that these reasons are fallacious. The committee decided to give five members to Toronto, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) says that we should have given Toronto more than five. The hon. gentleman from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) also argues very strongly, that members who represent outside constituencies, but who live in Toronto, are practically of no value to the city of Toronto, and he went so far as to name one member who occupies that position and who he said took little interest in matters affecting Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Who is that ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman mentioned the name of Sir William Mulock, in the committee, but to-night he has changed his ground, and he is willing to value a member living in a city and representing a rural constituency as being worth about one-half of the representatives of a city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: In this case they are elected by the people of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. member referred to the members for East York (Mr. Maclean) and for West York (Mr. Campbell), and I would be glad to know whether he regards them as each worth half a city member, or whether one is worth seven-eights and the other one-eighth. I take distinct issue with the hon. member (Mr1, Kemp) when lie says members living in Montreal or Toronto who represent outside constituencies are of no value to these cities. Every one in this House knows that when mutters affecting1 the welfare of the citizens of Toronto are discussed in this House the mem-366 i
bers who live in the city take a very keen interest in these questions. I have had a statement prepared which shows the number of members and the number of senators who live in the cities of Montreal and Toronto. I find in Toronto there are four senators

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Who are they ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Senators Aikens, Cox, [DOT]Tones and Kerr, and there are eight members of parliament living in- that city.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Who are the eight ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Messrs, Brock, Campbell, Clarke, Kemp, Maclean, McCarthy, Osier and Sir William Mulock.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Do the hon. members for West York and East York live in Toronto ?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows very well that to all intents and purposes they do. The hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean) has a suburban residence, but his business and interests are in the city. I do not think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) will seriously advance that argument. In Montreal there are ten senators and ten members living in that city. Toronto has twelve members and senators combined who are residents, and Montreal has twenty senators and members combined, a total of thirty-two for the two cities. Taking the average representation of Canada, I find there is one member for each 25,000 inhabitants, and taking the number of members living in Montreal and Toronto, I find there is one member for each 26,432. If that is a fair argument, the unit in Montreal and Toronto is only 1,432 less than in the rural constituencies. And when we combine members and senators, we find that on the average there is a representative in either House for a population of 18,331, while in the cities of Montreal and Toronto there is a member or a senator for each 14,867. In the case of the senators they practically represent no constituenciey and they have their business interests in the cities in which they live. And now as to the representation of the city of Toronto. Let usi see how far the unit of representation in that city as proposed by the present "Bill departs from the unit of representation established in 1892. In 1892 the unit for the whole province made up as in the present case, by taking the total population of Ontario, and deducting the city of Toronto, and dividing the quotient by the number of members, was 22.375, and the present unit is 24,381. In 1892 the city of Toronto was given four members. West Toronto with a population of 73,827, was given two members' making the unit 36,913. East Toronto with a population of 43,564, was given one member, Centre Toronto with a population of 26,632 was given one member. Take East Toronto, the largest constituency, with a unit of 43,564. Take the unit of represen-

tation for tbe whole province as 22,375, so that the Bill of 1892, so far as the largest constituency in Toronto was concerned, left a difference of 21,189, above the unit of the whole province. If you take the present Bill, you will find that the population of West Toronto is 44,991, of North Toronto 41,154, of Centre Toronto 43,861, of South Toronto 38,205, and of East Toronto 39,529. The largest unit proposed in the Bill is 44,991, and the unit for, the whole of Ontario is 24,381. Therefore applying exactly the same rule, the largest constituency of Toronto, is only 20,610 above the unit, as against 21,189 in 1892. There is a fair comparison. The Bill of 1892 departed from the unit by 21,182 and the present Bill departs from the unit by only 20,610 in the case of the largest Toronto constituency. It must be remembered that we are dealing with a fixed number of representatives. We had to deal with the losing of six representatives in the older parts of the province and the providing of three additional ones in the new districts of the province. Under these circumstances one must take into consideration what the effect would have been of giving the city of Toronto its full representation. It must be remembered that that was not done in 1881 or in 1891 ; and it is only fair to point out to the House that if we had undertaken to give the city of Toronto eight representatives, what the effect would have been upon the rural constituencies. The county of Northumberland would have lost a member, the county of Lanark would have lost a member, and the county of Peterborough would have lost a member. Unfortunately, these three constituencies happen to be in the eastern part of the province, and their representation would have been materially reduced. These were the main reasons which the committee took into consideration when they were giving the representation to the city of Toronto.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think any hon. gentleman on that side of the-House, when the question of the apportionment of members to the city of Toronto was under consideration in 1891, objected that the city was not getting justice. East Toronto had a population of 27,000. and West Toronto a population of 42,000. Instead of finding fault with their political complexion, they did not suppose that the arrangement would give any party advantage.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I was trying to make my argument apart from political considera-, tions.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman lias read the names of a number of members and senators who live in the city of Toronto and the city of Montreal. What has that, to do with the question ? Ail the members of the cabinet live in Ottawa from one end of the year to the other. If cue man has one vote, surely equal value must Mr. HYMAN.
be attached to each vote. If the unit of representation was above what it ought to have been in 1891, in view of the large increase in population which had taken place in Toronto since 1878, since the national policy was established, and if scant justice was done to the city of Toronto in 1891, what is being done now ? The unit of representation was 36,000 under the redistribution Act of that time, whereas the unit of representation under this Bill is almost 42,000. Is that justice and fair-play to the city of Toronto ? I leave it to the committee, and I will take the opportunity later of testing what is the feeling of the House upon it.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I do not think that is a fair representation to make. The hon. gentleman ought to take into account, not only Toronto, but East and West York as well. In 1891 these had a population of 221,064, and they were given six members, or one member to 36,866 people. Take the same territory to-day-Centre and South York, which represent East and West York, and the city of Toronto. There are 250,000 people to-day, and they are to have seven members, so that there will be a member for 35,700 people. We are reducing the unit of representation by 1,000, and I would ask the hon. member for West Toronto what justice or fairness there was in giving Centre Toronto a member for 26,600 people and giving West York, a large rural constituency, which extends twenty miles north, and at the same time embraces 25,000 of the city's population, one member for 41,000 people. Then, if you take the purely rural constituency of Peel, with 15,000 people, you give it one member. What sense of fairness was there In that ? How could you justify it ? And yet the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) tries to justify that, which was done in 1891, while to-day, as I have shown, we are giving the people of Toronto and the two Yorks a member for over 1,000 less than they had in 1891.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Surely that argument is not worthy of the hon. member. I am astonished that any man could get up and make such statements, when two of the members he refers to represent over 40,000 people each. It is. worse than childish.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It is not worth wasting the time of the committee upon. Tbe three members for York are to represent 64,023 people, which makes a unit of a little over 21,000, while each of the six city members will represent a unit of 42,000 people. Is that equitable or just to the city of Toronto?

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
It appears to me that no rule has ever been laid down with reference to the representation of cities in this country. A city like Toronto, which is about ten miles square, with five representatives, seems to me to be better represented than

a constituency like mine, which has 128,000 square miles, and only one representative. I understand that the hon. member for East Toronto has a big manufacturing institution, in which I suppose he would have 200 or 300 electors. I am sure it is much easier for him to attend to their wants than it is for the representative of a rural constituency to look after the interests of 150 or 200 farmers. So that I do not think any rule should be laid down as to the representation of cities. I think that the larger the city the larger the unit should be. When you get a compact population like that of the city of Toronto within an area of ten miles, it is well represented by five members, and judging by the character of the representatives that it has in this House, and the time they take up, it is very well represented. The hon. member for West Toronto, has told us that the member for East York is not a resident of the city. Well, lie ran as mayor a short time ago, and I think we can rightly consider him as a representative and resident of that city.
Item agreed to.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: Having disposed of York, I think we might adjourn.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: It was understood when York was disposed of the committee would rise and report progress.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I did not hear of any such arrangement.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: I was informed by the leader of the opposition that he had an understanding with the first Minister to that effect.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: When the Prime Minister left, he said to me, we will finish Ontario, and then we might adjourn.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: There will be a long debate on Toronto, and from what I understood from our leader was when York was finished we would adjourn.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We have discussed the whole matter as regards Toronto. Nearly all the arguments advanced have been advanced with regard to that city. There is no question regarding the redistribution of York. There is an amendment, but it has not been moved, and it only affects one small town.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext: We were told that as soon as we were through with York we might adjourn.

maintopic: REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.
speechtext:
Whatever understanding was come to should be observed, but I certainly did not understand the Prime Minister to agree to what the hon. member for East Grey suggests. However, if that be his impression, I move that the committee rise, and report progress, i
Progress reported.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CONGRATULATION TO PRIME MINISTER.

speechtext: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CONGRATULATION TO PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to avail myself of the opportunity on this, the anniversary of an important election which took place twenty-five years ago, of reminding the House of the situation to-day. I had lioped to have an opportunity of congratulating the right hon. the leader of the House on the fact that he has been consecutively here for the last twenty-five years, and also to congratulate him upon the continued health and strength both of body and mind which he enjoys, and the evidence he has given, every year up to the present, of his earnest desire to do the very best he could for the country. I may refer to the fact that I am the only member, I believe, who came in as a new member in 1878, who has been here consecutively ever since. There are only two others, the Hon. John Costigan and the Hon. John Haggart, who, besides the right hon. leader of the House, were here then, and have been ever since, so that time brings its changes in parliamentary as well as in other lines of life. May I be permitted to congratulate the country and the House as well on the changes which have taken place since twenty-five years ago, and especially on that great event, the inauguration of the national policy, which has resulted in such great good to the Dominion ? I congratulate this country also on the fact that those who fought that policy so vigorously at the outset and who are living to-day have become converts to that faith, and are carrying it out although not along the same intelligent and discreet lines as did its original inventors, and may I be permitted to refer to the fact as a passing tribute of respect to the great man who has long since gone to his last home, the late Sir John Macdonald. If he were alive to-day, we, the few who remain of those who served under him, would congratulate him on the policy he inaugurated, and congratulate the country on his prescience, as shown by the fact that all those who are in the House to-day which opposed him then have lived to become converts to that faith.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CONGRATULATION TO PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext:
I regret that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is not present to express his thanks for the very kind reference which the hon. member for East Grey has made to him. I am sure that he will regret his absence, but will appreciate, when he reads them in ' Hansard,' the very kind and flattering observations of my hon. friend. Passing from that to the national policy of that day and the alleged continuance of it, one cannot fail to wonder why, if it is the

national policy that we are continuing, hon. gentlemen opposite should be agitating the country to destroy it. If it be really the national policy, my hon. friend and his associates are doing themselves great injustice when they go up and down the country declaring that we must have a change of policy.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CONGRATULATION TO PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext: We want the policy developed and strengthened.

maintopic: ADJOURNMENT - CONGRATULATION TO PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext:
If we are to regard our policy as a contiuuauce of the national policy, I will repeat the suggestion once offered by my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, at a public meeting in my hearing :	If you, gentlemen, regard
this as the national policy, he said, you must be supremely grateful that it has passed from the hands of men who did not understand it into the hands of men capable of administering and developing it. and producing results so vastly to the good of Canada. Let me join in expressing our congratulations to my hon. friend from East Grey on having so long and continuously represented the people of Canada in this parliament. It is gratifying that among the many things which happen in political strife, there is always recognized on both sides long and faithful service, for, however we may differ in our views in political affairs, we recognize that all are labouring for the advancement of our common country.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.25 a.m., Friday.
Feiday, September 18, 1903.
